items.abstract: <jats:p>Dielectric barrier discharge (DBD) plasmas have attracted considerable interest in a wide range of applications. However, different applications often require specific electrode geometries, and conventional electrode patterning methods can be costly and time-consuming. Here, we demonstrate a simple, low-cost method for fabricating DBD-plasma devices using 3D-printed contact masks. A poly(lactic acid) (PLA) mask produced by fused deposition modeling (FDM) was placed on a dielectric barrier, and conductive paint was sprayed through the mask openings to form the high-voltage electrode. The process requires no vacuum equipment, cleanroom facilities, wet chemical etching, sintering, or laser processing, enabling rapid modification and fabrication of electrode designs. Using a single mask, we fabricated comb-shaped DBD devices on glass, polyimide (PI) film, and 3D-printed PLA dielectric barriers. The design flexibility of 3D printing also enabled the fabrication of a kirigami-inspired DBD device that could be folded through 180° while maintaining plasma operation. These results demonstrate the potential of 3D-printed contact masks for the rapid, low-cost fabrication of application-specific DBD-plasma devices. The main limitations of the method are a coarser edge definition than screen or inkjet printing and the limited heat and erosion resistance of polymer barriers, which restrict the devices to burst-mode, short-duration operation.</jats:p>
title: Facile Fabrication of Dielectric Barrier Discharge Plasma Device by 3D-Printed Contact Mask

items.abstract: <jats:p>Motivated by quantum-gravity scenarios involving possible black-hole to white-hole-like transitions, we introduce a minimal phenomenological model in which black-hole evolution is associated with a creation pressure that may contribute to cosmic acceleration without a fundamental cosmological constant. Within the standard FLRW framework, black holes are represented by their averaged energy density, while local strong-gravity effects are neglected. The proposed mechanism links the cumulative effects of black-hole growth to an effective negative-pressure contribution. The model is exploratory and does not claim observational confirmation. In particular, the creation-pressure law remains an assumption whose microscopic origin in black-hole physics and associated energy budget require further investigation.</jats:p>
title: Could Black Holes Drive the Acceleration of the Universe? An Idealized Approach

items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Global (zero-dimensional or spatially averaged) models are widely employed to study complex chemistries in low-temperature plasmas (LTPs). By adopting a spatially average description of the plasma, they substantially reduce the computational cost while still providing reliable and detailed insight into the key processes taking place in the plasma. In their most general formulation, global models (GM) involve the coupled solution of a Boltzmann solver (to describe the electron kinetics) and a Chemistry solver (to describe the heavy-species kinetics). This paper presents a tutorial on the LisbOn KInetics Global Model (LoKI-GM) framework, developed in MATLAB and available as open-source code. The framework couples the Boltzmann solver LoKI-B, which solves the space-independent form of the two-term electron Boltzmann equation for non-magnetized non-equilibrium LTPs, excited by DC/HF electric fields or time-dependent (non-oscillatory) electric fields, and the Chemistry solver LoKI-C, which solves the system of zero-dimensional rate balance equations for the main charged and neutral species in the plasma and at the surface, receiving as input the kinetic schemes for the gas/plasma/surface system under study. Distinctive features of LoKI-GM include the closure of the model through charge neutrality, which yields the self-consistent maintenance field of DC and HF discharges, and the availability of several transport models for charged and neutral species. LoKI-GM can also couple a microkinetic mesoscopic surface model and a gas thermal model to the volume kinetics. We briefly present the formulation of LoKI-GM, including its numerical solution strategy, input/output parameters, and calculation workflow for both active discharges and afterglow plasmas. The main differences with respect to existing GM are highlighted, and the flexibility of the code for plasma chemistry studies is demonstrated through representative simulation results obtained across a range of gas discharge configurations and operating conditions.</jats:p>
title: LoKI-GM: a global model framework for plasma chemistry studies

items.abstract: <jats:p>Acceleration-induced loss of consciousness (G-LOC) remains a critical threat to high-performance aircraft pilots, primarily driven by cerebral hypoperfusion and subsequent hypoxia. Current physiological monitoring systems fail to reliably identify or predict these events. This narrative review explores the potential of exhaled breath volatile organic compound (VOC) analysis as a non-invasive, real-time monitoring solution for G-LOC detection. The pathophysiology of G-LOC, encompassing acute cerebral hypoxia, oxidative stress, lipid peroxidation, and distinct hemodynamic shifts, could produce measurable alterations in breath VOC profiles, although this has not yet been demonstrated during G-LOC itself. Candidate biomarkers derived from hypoxia research include isoprene, which reflects acute hemodynamic changes, alongside oxidative stress and lipid peroxidation products such as pentanal, 4-butyrolactone, and pentane. To effectively monitor these volatile signatures, the selection of analytical platforms must balance sensitivity, specificity, and operational feasibility. This review evaluates current technologies, proposing a multi-tiered approach: Gas Chromatography-Mass Spectrometry (GC-MS) for comprehensive biomarker discovery, Selected Ion Flow Tube-Mass Spectrometry (SIFT-MS) and Proton Transfer Reaction-Mass Spectrometry (PTR-MS) for targeted, real-time validation, and Electronic Nose (E-Nose) systems as a potential, yet unvalidated, option for portable in-flight deployment. However, the current evidence is indirect, derived mainly from min-long hypoxia exposures rather than from the seconds-long hypoperfusion of G-LOC, and it remains unknown whether a G-LOC-related volatile signal reaches exhaled breath quickly enough to allow detection, let alone prediction. We therefore outline the main knowledge gaps and propose a stepwise research roadmap to address them.</jats:p>

items.abstract: <jats:p>Real-time process monitoring during high-speed laser drilling remains a critical challenge in modern manufacturing, where industrial laser systems operate at repetition rates of up to several hundred kilohertz [D. Franz et al., Materials 15, 3932 (2022)], with next-generation systems targeting the megahertz regime [S. Janssen et al., Proc. SPIE 13350, 1335007 (2025)]. As each ablating laser pulse creates a tiny plasma with material-specific emission lines, laser-induced breakdown spectroscopy could be used to enable process monitoring. However, existing laser-induced breakdown spectroscopy (LIBS) approaches so far are limited to kilohertz acquisition rates [R. Noll, Laser-Induced Breakdown Spectroscopy: Fundamentals and Applications (Springer, Berlin, 2012)], three orders of magnitude too slow for inline monitoring and closed-loop control at industrial processing speeds. We present a high-speed LIBS sensor capable of per-pulse material analysis at repetition rates exceeding 1 MHz, enabling real-time feedback during laser microvia drilling in printed circuit boards (PCBs). The system detects the copper atomic emission line at 521.8 nm using a narrow bandpass filter combined with high-speed photodetection and custom analog signal processing, achieving complete signal acquisition within the 1 μs interpulse period at 1 MHz. Time-resolved plasma emission characterization reveals the nanosecond-scale temporal dynamics and validates the temporal gating approach for background suppression. Comprehensive validation against conventional spectrometer-based LIBS across multilayer PCB structures demonstrates equivalent material classification performance, confirmed by laser scanning microscopy. Microvia drilling experiments with position-resolved material detection demonstrate accurate real-time material classification throughout the drilling process. A retrospective analysis of the acquired position-resolved data indicates that applying a closed-loop termination strategy could reduce laser pulse count by 18.6% on average and up to 25.6% in favorable cases, compared to conventional fixed-pulse protocols. These results establish MHz-rate LIBS as a viable approach for inline quality control and adaptive process feedback at time scales relevant to industrial laser micromachining.</jats:p>
title: Pulse-resolved laser-induced breakdown spectroscopy for inline monitoring of microvia drilling in printed circuit boards at MHz repetition rates

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Large-scale inspection requires both dense surface data and a stable global reference, which are difficult to obtain with a single instrument. This paper proposes a joint measurement method integrating a laser scanner, a stereo-vision tracking unit, and a laser tracker. In the proposed method, the scanner captures dense local surface data, the stereo-vision unit determines the scanner pose, and the laser tracker establishes the global reference by observing a scanner-mounted spherically mounted retroreflector (SMR). Paired observations of the same SMR center connect the tracking and laser-tracker frames, forming a unified coordinate chain that transforms local point clouds into the global frame. To ensure the accuracy of this joint measurement chain, a depth-stratified calibration-position design is further introduced to account for distance-dependent stereo uncertainty. The 3–6 m working volume is divided into near, middle, and far ranges, and eleven 12-position layouts are assessed by Monte Carlo simulation and repeated experiments. The results show that middle-dominated mixed-depth layouts consistently achieve low error levels, with the 3/6/3 (S7) and 2/8/2 (S8) near/middle/far configurations showing particularly favorable performance. For S7, the mean SMR-center consistency residuals are 0.101 mm and 0.106 mm for the fixed and estimated SMR-center modes, respectively, corresponding to reductions of 13.1% and 11.5% relative to the near-only layout. These results support distance-aware calibration-position planning for the 3–6 m, 12-position configuration investigated in this study and the proposed cross-system coordinate framework.</jats:p>
title: A joint measurement method integrating stereo-vision-tracked laser scanning and laser-tracker referencing: depth-stratified calibration-position design

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>To compare the real-world outcomes of a novel navigated panretinal photocoagulation (PRP) laser system with a modified wavelength of 577 nm and variable pulse duration with conventional argon laser PRP in retinal vasoproliferative disease.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Retrospective single-center cohort study of eyes treated with PRP for proliferative diabetic retinopathy (DR), central retinal vein occlusion (CRVO) or other ischemic retinopathies. Argon laser PRP (2017–2020; argon laser cohort, ALC17/20) was compared with a navigated PRP laser system used at short pulse durations in two periods (navigated laser cohorts 2018–2020, NLC18/20, and 2022–2024, NLC22/24, after an in-house protocol change). The primary endpoint was retreatment-free survival; secondary endpoints were vitrectomy-free survival and laser parameters. Cox models were adjusted for age, indication, baseline disease severity and prior anti-VEGF treatment, with robust variance accounting for the inclusion of both eyes.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      A total of 497 eyes of 375 patients were included (ALC17/20: 160, NLC18/20: 206 and NLC22/24: 131 eyes). Compared to ALC17/20, navigated PRP used more pulses (median 1,542 in NLC18/20 and 2,043 in NLC22/24 vs 867 in ALC17/20), shorter pulses (30.0 ms in NLC18/20 and 23.8 ms in NLC22/24 vs 135.9 ms in ALC17/20) and less total energy (13,572 mJ in NLC18/20 and 15,645 mJ in NLC22/24 vs 28,403 mJ in ALC17/20, all
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       < 0.001). Two-year retreatment-free survival was 72.2% in ALC17/20, 62.0% in NLC18/20 and 42.7% in NLC22/24. After adjustment for age, indication, baseline disease severity and prior anti-VEGF treatment, the risk of retreatment was not significantly increased in NLC18/20 (HR 1.37, 95% CI 0.91–2.05) compared to the ALC17/20 group, but remained increased in NLC22/24 (HR 2.38, 1.59–3.56), indicating a worse clinical outcome in this cohort; this finding was robust in landmark, time-split and weighted analyses. Vitrectomy rates did not differ (adjusted HR 1.28 in NLC18/20 and 1.16 in NLC22/24). Neovascularization of the disc or elsewhere, younger age and worse visual acuity were independently associated with retreatment rates, whereas pulse duration, total energy and number of sessions showed non-significant trends only.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Navigated PRP required more secondary interventions than argon laser PRP, partly because eyes with more active disease were more often selected for the new system; even after accounting for this, more retreatments were needed, indicating insufficient initial treatment. Vitrectomy rates did not differ. New laser systems should be accompanied by systematic evaluation of their efficacy and patient selection, and treatment protocols adapted accordingly.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Comparison of panretinal scatter photocoagulation in retinal vasoproliferative disease using argon laser vs navigated laser photocoagulation

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>We present a high-repetition-rate experimental platform for proton stopping-power measurements in warm dense matter (WDM) in a regime where the projectile velocity approaches the electron thermal velocity and theoretical predictions remain highly uncertain. The platform combines laser-driven proton generation via target normal sheath acceleration with a compact magnetic energy selector to produce quasi-monoenergetic proton beams in the 0.3–0.6 MeV range with energy bandwidths of tens of keV and sub-nanosecond duration. WDM is generated by femtosecond laser heating of thin carbon foils and characterized using streaked optical pyrometry and x-ray pinhole grating spectroscopy, supported by radiation-hydrodynamic simulations. We investigate the present limitations of the approach, including uncertainties in sample conditions, finite proton bunch duration, and proton scattering, and discuss pathways toward improved measurements. The results demonstrate a versatile and scalable approach for systematic, high-statistics studies of ion stopping power in WDM relevant to inertial confinement fusion and charged-particle transport in high-energy-density plasmas.</jats:p>
title: Platform for high repetition rate proton stopping power measurements in warm dense matter

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    Nonstorm‐time relativistic electron acceleration has attracted considerable attention, yet the competitive contributions of radial diffusion and local diffusion remain to be fully understood. Here we perform 3‐D numerical modeling to investigate a rapid enhancement event of electron phase space densities (PSDs) for
                    <jats:italic>μ</jats:italic>
                     = 500–2,500 MeV/G at high
                    <jats:italic>L</jats:italic>
                    * during the substorm‐active nonstorm period from January 13 to 15, 2013. Comparing the simulation results with Van Allen Probes observations, we reveal that radial diffusion and chorus wave scattering exhibit significant energy‐dependent contributions to the relativistic electron acceleration. Specifically, the simulations using two different radial diffusion models, together with simultaneous ULF wave observations, indicate that radial diffusion plays a critical role in the enhancements of electron PSDs for
                    <jats:italic>μ</jats:italic>
                     < 2,000 MeV/G at
                    <jats:italic>L</jats:italic>
                    * > ∼4.5. In contrast, chorus waves primarily accelerate higher‐energy electrons with
                    <jats:italic>μ</jats:italic>
                     = 2000–2,500 MeV/G at
                    <jats:italic>L</jats:italic>
                    * > ∼5. Moreover, the synergy of both mechanisms facilitates acceleration more effectively than either alone and can well reproduce the location and magnitude of the enhanced PSDs for
                    <jats:italic>μ</jats:italic>
                     = 500–2,500 MeV/G. Our study provides new insights into the competitive interplay between radial diffusion and chorus wave scattering in substorm‐active nonstorm‐time acceleration of outer zone relativistic electrons.
                  </jats:p>
title: Outer Radiation Belt Electron Acceleration During a Substorm‐Active Nonstorm Interval: Energy‐Dependent Roles of Radial Diffusion and Chorus Waves

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Driven by recent discoveries regarding the quantum Mpemba effect, the anomalous relaxation dynamics of open quantum systems have garnered significant attention. While expediting thermalization to equilibrium has been extensively studied, dynamically accelerating the convergence toward nonequilibrium steady states remains a formidable challenge. In this Letter, we find that a transiently engineered nonreciprocal dissipative channel can provide a shortcut that accelerates relaxation to the target reciprocal nonequilibrium steady state. Using a two-mode interacting bosonic model, we demonstrate that the temporal activation of a nonreciprocal channel efficiently suppresses prolonged inter-mode energy oscillations, enforcing a rapid, unidirectional thermal dump into the environment. Counterintuitively, under symmetric local dissipation, both nonreciprocal directions exhibit relaxation speedup with identical asymptotic spectral decay rates. Our results establish a route to accelerated nonequilibrium steady-state preparation in the studied bosonic model, with a covariance-based sufficient condition that extends to a multimode chain.</jats:p>
title: Nonreciprocal Relaxation Acceleration

<jats:p>Objetivo: Determinar la correlación entre el Índice Aterogénico del Plasma (IAP) y el Péptido Natriurético tipo B (BNP) en pacientes con Insuficiencia Cardíaca Crónica Agudizada.


Material y métodos: Estudio transversal, correlacional, analítico. A través de un muestreo no probabilístico, fueron evaluados pacientes con insuficiencia cardíaca crónica agudizada, con medición al ingreso de BNP, perfil de lípidos y a quienes fue realizado un ecocardiograma transtorácico durante su hospitalización.


Resultados: Fueron estudiados 30 pacientes con insuficiencia cardíaca agudizada. La mediana de los niveles de BNP al ingreso fue de 764.5 pg/mL, la mediana del IAP fue de 0.51. La media de la fracción de eyección del ventrículo izquierdo (FEVI) obtenida fue de 38%, todos los pacientes presentaron algún grado de disfunción diastólica: el 50% grado 1, el 33.3% grado 2 y sólo el 16.6% grado 3. El coeficiente de correlación de Spearman para el BNP e IAP fue de -0,02213, con un valor de p=0.5.


Conclusiones: El IAP juega un papel como un factor de riesgo cardiovascular, pero no como parte de la evaluación de los pacientes con Insuficiencia Cardíaca Crónica Agudizada. No existe correlación entre el IAP y BNP.</jats:p>
title: Correlación entre el índice aterogénico del plasma y el péptido natriurético tipo B en pacientes con insuficiencia cardíaca cronica agudizada

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Recurrent functional tongue restriction after previous lingual frenectomies presents a clinical challenge, particularly when earlier surgical records are unavailable.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Case presentation</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A 22-year-old woman reported two previous scalpel frenectomies followed by recurrent restriction of tongue mobility. Before reintervention, maximum mouth opening was 51 mm, whereas opening with the tongue tip touching the incisive papilla was 16 mm (31.37%). Management comprised surgical release with a 980-nm high-power diode laser, histopathological examination of the excised tissue, perioperative photobiomodulation (808 nm before surgery and 660 nm afterward), and postoperative orofacial myofunctional therapy. Histopathology showed collagen-rich tissue consistent with fibrosis but could not establish its cause. Tongue-to-papilla opening increased to 29 mm immediately after surgery and measured 27 mm at eight months, an 11-mm improvement relative to baseline. At approximately 23 months, clinical examination showed a healed surgical site without clinically evident anterior frenulum reattachment; the patient reported satisfactory oral function without perceived recurrent tongue restriction. No standardized quantitative tongue-mobility measurement was obtained at this later visit.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This case documents favorable clinical and patient-reported findings after a multimodal reintervention. The individual contributions of laser surgery, photobiomodulation, and myofunctional therapy cannot be determined from a single case.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: High-power diode laser-assisted reintervention for recurrent fibrotic ankyloglossia following two scalpel frenectomies: a case report with 23​-month follow-up

                    , are compared to simulation results. Ion-neutral cross section data, commonly used in previous work, are found to provide a limited accuracy for the ion dynamics and conversion in the sheaths, resulting in ion flux energy distribution functions at the electrodes that differ significantly from measured data. In agreement with more recent datasets, the ion–neutral cross sections are, therefore, scaled to reproduce the experimental results. The coefficients for ion–ion recombination, secondary electron emission, and electron reflection at the electrodes are systematically varied to achieve precise alignment with the measured plasma properties including the accurate description of electron power absorption mode transitions as a function of the driving voltage amplitude. The choice of the ion–ion recombination coefficient is found to have a strong effect on this mode transition in the simulation. With these key input parameters adjusted, good quantitative agreement between simulation and experimental results is achieved over a wide range of external control parameters providing the basis for quantitatively accurate digital-twin plasma simulations.

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Introduction: Sudden sensorineural hearing loss (SSNHL) is an acute auditory disorder with a largely idiopathic origin and unpredictable clinical outcomes. There is a need for objective biomarkers to elucidate the pathophysiology of the disease. This study aimed to explore the plasma metabolomic profile of patients with unilateral idiopathic SSNHL (uiSSNHL) and identify disease-associated metabolic alterations, elucidating underlying pathophysiologic mechanisms. Methods: A total of 40 uiSSNHL patients and 40 age- and sex-matched healthy controls were enrolled. Plasma samples were analyzed using untargeted liquid chromatography–mass spectrometry (LC-MS). Statistical analysis included principal component analysis and volcano plot generation, with adjustments for age, sex and body mass index. Based on identified metabolites, metabolic pathway-enrichment analysis was conducted. Results: Multivariate analysis revealed a distinct metabolic profile in the uiSSNHL group compared to controls. Among 1045 detected metabolites, 388 showed significant differences, 195 were significantly elevated and 193 were significantly reduced. Notably, N-acetyl-L-phenylalanine, hypoxanthine, and tryptophan-related compounds were upregulated, while bilirubin, oleoylethanolamide, and carnitine-related metabolites were downregulated. These findings implicate disruptions in amino acid metabolism, oxidative stress regulation, purine degradation, and lipid signaling in the pathophysiology of uiSSNHL. Conclusions: Patients with uiSSNHL exhibit distinct plasma metabolomic alterations involving multiple biological pathways. These metabolites may serve as potential biomarkers and offer insights into the systemic processes underlying SSNHL, providing a foundation for future diagnostic and therapeutic strategies.</jats:p>
title: Plasma metabolomic analysis in patients with sudden sensorineural hearing loss

<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Severely calcified coronary lesions remain a major challenge during percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI), frequently resulting in difficulty with device crossing, inadequate lesion preparation, stent delivery, and lastly stent under‐expansion. Intravascular imaging provides important information regarding the extent and distribution of coronary calcium and can guide in selecting appropriate calcium modification strategy. Excimer laser coronary atherectomy (ELCA) is an established adjunctive technique that may be useful in selected balloon‐uncrossable lesions as well as in refractory stent under‐expansion.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Case Summary</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      A 52‐year‐old man with diabetes mellitus and hypertension presented with chest discomfort since 1 day, with electrocardiographic changes, a significantly positive Troponin value and normal ejection fraction. In view of clinical presentation of acute coronary syndrome, a coronary angiography was done which demonstrated calcific multivessel coronary artery disease with a 95% calcific stenosis of the proximal left anterior descending (LAD) artery and an 80% distal LAD stenosis. After balloon pre dilatation, saline ELCA (0.9‐mm catheter; fluence 50, rate 60) facilitated IVUS crossing. A 3.0 × 38‐mm drug‐eluting stent was deployed in the ostioproximal LAD but remained significantly under‐expanded despite high‐pressure balloon dilatation. Repeat ELCA followed by further balloon dilatation resulted in good stent expansion, with a final IVUS minimum stent area of 7.2 mm
                      <jats:sup>2</jats:sup>
                      and TIMI 3 flow without residual stenosis or complications. The patient remained well at 6‐month follow‐up.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: From Uncrossable to Under‐Expanded: A Dual Role for Excimer Laser in Complex Calcific LAD PCI

items.abstract: <jats:p>Laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) Ti–6Al–4V shows orientation-dependent fatigue behavior that tensile properties and bulk density do not fully explain. Vertical (VT) and horizontal (HZ) specimens were annealed at 850 °C for 2 h (furnace cooling) and characterized by optical and scanning electron microscopy, X-ray diffraction (XRD) with Rietveld refinement, micro-computed tomography (micro-CT), Vickers hardness, tensile tests, and high-cycle fatigue tests (R = 0.1). The annealed material consisted of α + β (approximately 88–92 vol.% α and 8–12 vol.% β). Tensile properties of the two orientations were similar, with HZ specimens slightly stronger and of similar elongation. Despite a bulk density above 99.9%, micro-CT revealed isolated pores of roughly 60–270 μm. At 600 MPa, VT specimens failed after 6.79 × 104 and 7.36 × 104 cycles, whereas HZ specimens failed after 8.82 × 105 and 1.37 × 106 cycles. Fatigue data at other stress levels are limited, so the orientation effect is demonstrated only at 600 MPa, where two specimens per orientation were tested. The results indicate that defect size, morphology, and orientation relative to the load, rather than tensile properties or density, are the likely cause of the anisotropy. An orientation-sensitive descriptor, F = dmax cos2θ, is proposed as a hypothesis; specimen-resolved defect data exist for only three VT specimens, so it remains to be validated. No as-built control was tested, and conclusions apply to the annealed condition.</jats:p>
title: Defect-Related Fatigue Anisotropy in Laser Powder Bed Fusion Ti–6Al–4V: Role of Sub-β-Transus Annealing and Build Orientation

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Objective: to evaluate the relationship between enteral protein intake and plasma urea concentrations in preterm infants beyond 21 days of life (DOL) and determine whether plasma urea is a reliable marker of protein intake when accounting for potential nonlinear associations. Methods: prospective observational study that included a total of 110 preterm infants (&lt;36 weeks’ gestation) contributing 357 paired assessments of enteral nutritional intake and plasma urea concentrations obtained after 21 DOL. The main outcome measures the association between enteral protein intake (g/kg/day) and plasma urea concentration (mg/dL), assessed using robust linear regression, and generalized additive models. Results: Protein intake ranged from 1 to 6.9 g/kg/day and showed a weak positive correlation with plasma urea concentration (rho=0.24). In robust linear regression, plasma urea increased by 2.4±0.7 mg/dL for each additional 1g/kg/day of protein intake; however, the model explained only 4% of the variability in plasma urea concentrations (R–squared (R²)=0.04; Root Mean Square Error (RMSE)=10.1mg/dL). GAM analysis suggested a nonlinear relationship, but explanatory capacity remained low (R²=0.07; RMSE=9.8mg/dL). Adjustment for postmenstrual age and energy intake did not improve model performance. In a predefined subgroup analysis restricted to protein intakes &lt;4.5g/kg/day, no meaningful association was observed. Conclusions: plasma urea concentrations showed only a weak and poorly explanatory association with enteral protein intake in preterm infants beyond the early postnatal period. The relationship appeared nonlinear at higher protein intakes and was not evident within the currently recommended protein intake range, suggesting that plasma urea should not be used as a standalone surrogate marker of protein intake.</jats:p>
title: Plasma urea and enteral protein intake in preterm infants after the early postnatal period

                  <jats:p>
                    High‐quality white light sources for laser‐driven projection displays face a shortage of efficient, stable red‐emitting phosphors. To address this, a garnet‐structured orange‐emitting phosphor BaLu

To reduce heat accumulation under high‐power‐density blue laser excitation, the phosphor was co‐sintered as a film onto a sapphire plate and formed into a phosphor wheel. Optimizing h‐BN addition (serving as a heat spreader and light scatterer), sintering temperature, and phosphor‐to‐glass ratio yielded an optimal phosphor‐in‐glass film (PiGF) achieving a luminous flux of 1735.5 lm under 22 W blue laser excitation. The patterned PiGF, composing of spatially separated green‐emitting LuAG: Ce
                    <jats:sup>3+</jats:sup>

When subjected to identical power blue laser excitation, the prototype laser projection system equipped with this patterned PiGF exhibits visibly richer and more vivid color reproduction compared with projection device adopting conventional single‐component YAG:Ce
                    <jats:sup>3+</jats:sup>

items.abstract: <jats:p>Background and Objectives: We evaluated vaginal hyaluronic acid (HA) and Er:YAG for genitourinary syndrome of menopause (GSM) after cancer, separating treatment from prevention. Materials and Methods: We searched PubMed, CENTRAL, Scopus, Web of Science, CINAHL, ClinicalTrials.gov and WHO ICTRP on 20–24 August 2026 without date or language limits. Two reviewers independently confirmed eligibility and assessed risk of bias. We linked reports from the same study and grouped findings by intervention, cancer treatment, comparator and follow-up. Clinical and methodological heterogeneity precluded pooling. We used structured narrative synthesis and assessed certainty with GRADE. Results: From 1680 records, we identified 38 reports of 27 studies (nine randomised, four non-randomised comparative and 14 uncontrolled). Twenty-one studies evaluated HA and seven evaluated Er:YAG, including one trial comparing the two. All seven Er:YAG studies enrolled breast-cancer survivors. Three prevention/mixed-baseline trials formed a post hoc supplementary stratum. In the largest moisturiser trial (100 randomised; 88 analysed), HA/polycarbophil yielded higher Vaginal Health Index scores at 16 weeks (unadjusted mean difference of 3.90; 95% confidence interval of 2.71–5.09), but individual dryness and dyspareunia comparisons did not demonstrate superiority over lubricant. Er:YAG superiority over HA was not demonstrated; no randomised sham/no-treatment comparison was identified. Substantial risk of bias limited interpretation. Certainty was low or very low, and safety ascertainment was incomplete. Conclusions: HA-containing products may improve selected outcomes, but benefits are formulation-specific and uncertain. Preventive findings cannot establish treatment efficacy for existing GSM. Er:YAG-specific efficacy and durability remain unresolved. The available studies cannot establish long-term safety for either intervention. Registration: PROSPERO CRD420261481773. Funding: No external funding.</jats:p>
title: Nonhormonal Management of Genitourinary Syndrome of Menopause in Female Cancer Survivors: A Systematic Review of Vaginal Hyaluronic Acid and Er:YAG Laser Therapy

items.abstract: <jats:p>Femtosecond laser welding enables the direct joining of transparent materials through localized energy deposition and melting at the interface. However, achieving high joint strength and welding over large areas remain challenging due to high thermal gradients generated during processing, which can lead to crack appearance. In this study, N-BK7 glass was irradiated using a femtosecond laser source emitting 500 fs pulses at 1030 nm to investigate the influence of energy deposition and temporal pulse distribution on laser-induced modifications. Repetitive single-pulse irradiation was compared to burst modes operating at 40 MHz and 1.28 GHz. In-volume modifications were characterized as a function of pulse or burst energy, scanning velocity, and the number of pulses per burst. The resulting modification morphologies were classified to establish process maps and identify parameter ranges that minimize defect formation and are suitable for welding. Based on these findings, the repetitive single-pulse mode was selected to weld N-BK7 glass assemblies over a diameter of 20 mm, including configurations with peripheral welds. Shear tests performed on smaller welded areas yielded a maximum shear strength of 640 MPa. These results demonstrate the potential of femtosecond laser welding for the assembly of large-scale optical components.</jats:p>
title: Femtosecond Laser Welding of N-BK7 Glass: From In-Volume Modification to Large-Scale, High-Strength Joining

items.abstract: <jats:p>Whether metal sheets perforate under continuous-wave laser irradiation may depend on when energy is delivered, even when total prescribed energy and peak power are unchanged. Establishing this dependence is necessary to assess whether perforation thresholds can be transferred between power histories. We investigated this question using four power profiles on 2 mm thick 2A12 aluminum alloy sheets, with three independent specimens per profile. All exposures lasted 10 s, with a prescribed energy input of 30 kJ, and used a 40 mm spot diameter. High-speed imaging, rear-surface apparent temperatures, and post-test morphology characterized visible melting and perforation. The decisive comparison used time-reversed ramp-up/hold and hold/ramp-down profiles with the same 4 kW peak and time spent at each power level. All ramp-up/hold specimens perforated, whereas none of the hold/ramp-down specimens perforated within 10 s, despite earlier visible melting under hold/ramp-down. All ramp-up/ramp-down specimens also perforated, whereas none exposed to constant power at 3 kW did. Mean melting-to-perforation intervals were 1.47 s for ramp-up/ramp-down and 1.94 s for ramp-up/hold, coinciding with mean prescribed stage powers of 4.78 and 4.00 kW, respectively. These results demonstrate a loading-sequence effect under the tested conditions: total prescribed energy, peak power, and visible melting onset alone do not determine perforation outcome. Sustained power after visible melting may favor further melting and local thinning, although the underlying mechanisms and possible contributions from surface variability remain unresolved.</jats:p>
title: Effects of Continuous-Wave Laser Power History on Post-Melting Perforation of 2A12 Aluminum Alloy Sheets

Without vorticity, the problem is degenerate: arbitrary profiles travel without distortion at a field-determined speed and are neutrally stable. items.abstract: <jats:p>We investigate nonreciprocal single-photon transport in a cavity-mediated giant-atom waveguide-QED system with periodically modulated atom–cavity couplings. Two distinct mechanisms for directional transport are demonstrated within a unified interference framework. In the chiral regime, asymmetric coupling combined with the propagation-phase interference produces multiple frequency-selective isolation windows. In the nonchiral regime, periodic modulation generates a complex inter-cavity coupling with a controllable synthetic gauge phase, enabling the isolation frequency and preferred transmission direction to be dynamically tuned. Static atom–cavity coupling further reconstructs the Floquet-dressed spectrum and extends the accessible nonreciprocal frequency range. We also show that finite dissipation is essential for converting direction-dependent coherent interference into a pronounced transmission contrast in both regimes. These results establish a unified route to structurally induced and dynamically reconfigurable single-photon nonreciprocity for quantum routing and directional photonic interfaces.</jats:p>
title: Chiral and Floquet-induced single-photon nonreciprocity in a cavity-mediated giant-atom waveguide-QED system

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Relativistic electron losses in the outer radiation belt are mainly attributed to outward radial transport and wave–particle resonant interactions, two mechanisms that are incorporated into modern radiation belt simulations. Although the effect of field‐line curvature scattering (FLCS) on the loss of energetic electrons at the nightside edge of the outer radiation belt has been recognized, its efficiency has not yet been thoroughly investigated. In this study, we present an analysis of relativistic and ultra‐relativistic electron measurements onboard the International Space Station (ISS), with the orbit nominally well inside the outer radiation belt. Using data from the Calorimetric Electron Telescope (CALET) and the Monitor of All‐sky X‐ray Image (MAXI) onboard the ISS, we distinguish FLCS events from those associated with electron losses driven by wave activity. We demonstrate that CALET can detect events involving  MeV electron losses due to FLCS. These events are long‐lasting, indicating that FLCS can provide continuous electron losses over timescales of several hours. We also discuss the potential role of the FLCS mechanism in outer radiation belt dynamics.</jats:p>
title: Operation of Field‐Line Curvature Scattering Mechanism Deep Inside the Outer Radiation Belt: Observations Onboard ISS

<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Twisted graphene bilayers exhibit rich physical phenomena under external fields, yet the coupled effect of electric fields and interlayer sliding on their charge distribution remains elusive. By combining first-principles calculations with a machine learning technique, we systematically investigate interlayer sliding-induced charge transfer and redistribution in both twisted and AB-stacked graphene bilayers under vertical electric fields. Unlike the homogeneous charge distribution observed in AB-stacked bilayers, the heterogeneous charge distribution in certain twisted graphene bilayers exhibits robust insensitivity to applied electric fields, even under strong fields up to 2 V/nm. This field insensitivity enables such twisted bilayers to maintain ultralow interlayer friction under extreme bias conditions. To quantitatively describe the coupled effect of interlayer sliding and electric fields on interlayer charge transfer and friction, we develop a charge-modified registry index (RICM) model for graphene bilayers. The revealed electric-field insensitivity in specific twisted configurations can be mainly attributed to the inherently small variation in the maximum registry index change (∆RICM) under bias, providing a simple descriptor for designing low-friction interfaces in electrically gated graphene devices.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Robust insensitivity of heterogeneous charge distribution and interlayer friction to strong external electric fields in twisted graphene bilayers

It is well known that the sample means in the Strong Law of Large Numbers can converge arbitrarily slowly. The convergence of ergodic averages also suffers from such ineffectiveness, and in this situation a prominent way to study the quantitative nature of the convergence of such processes is through looking at the stochastic fluctuations or oscillations . As the Pointwise Ergodic Theorem generalises the Strong Law of Large Numbers when the random variables are independent identically distributed, the quantitative oscillatory results from ergodic theory carry over naturally to this setting.

We initiate the investigation of the oscillatory behaviour of the averages in the Strong Law of Large Numbers in the case where the random variables carry dependencies. In this paper, we consider the case where the random variables are pairwise independent and construct learnable rates of uniform convergence . This notion, introduced by the author and Powell, strengthens Tao’s notion of metastability and provides a quantitative bound on how far one must look to locate a region of local stability (that is, a region with no oscillations) with high probability.
title: Oscillations in the Strong Law of Large Numbers

<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Introduction</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Undertaking a successful direct repair of a chronic pectoralis major (PM) tear can be challenging. We undertook a direct repair, including a muscle release from the underlying ribs if required, on a series of patients with chronic PM tears.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Materials and methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Between November 2019 and May 2022, patients who underwent a chronic PM tear repair were reviewed. Pre-operative and final follow-up function was assessed using the Bak Score, Oxford Shoulder Score (OSS) and Single Assessment Numeric Evaluation (SANE) scores.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Twenty patients were available at final follow-up. The mean age was 34.5 years (18–59), mean surgery delay was 9.3 months (1.5–32) and the mean follow-up was 31.3 months (25–55). At surgery, nine patients required a release of the muscle belly from the ribs. At final follow-up, the Bak scores were 13 (65%) for excellent and 7 (35%) for good; the mean pre-operative OSS rose from 33.9 (24–48) to 47.9 (46–48) and the mean SANE score rose from 42.5 (10–100) to 91.3 (70–100). There was no clinical evidence of any re-ruptures.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>For patients with a chronic PM rupture, undertaking an extensive mobilisation with a muscle release, as required, provides a satisfactory outcome with regards to construct survival, clinical outcomes and return to sport.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Level of evidence</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>IV – Case Series.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Functional outcome and return to sport following direct repair of chronic pectoralis major rupture

items.abstract: <jats:p>To investigate the compaction characteristics and dynamic response of sandstone fill subgrades under strong vibration conditions, field vibratory compaction tests were conducted based on an in-service expressway project under different numbers of passes and rolling speeds. Tri-axial accelerometers were embedded within the subgrade to continuously monitor the internal dynamic response signals during the compaction process. Combined with the degree of compaction obtained from the sand-cone method, a systematic analysis was performed on the dynamic characteristics and compaction performance of the sandstone subgrade during strong vibratory compaction. The results indicate that the sandstone subgrade exhibits pronounced differences in dynamic response during vibratory compaction. The horizontal acceleration is strongly influenced by particle rearrangement and shear action of the fill material, and its variation is highly sensitive to the compaction process. With an increasing number of passes, the internal acceleration response of the subgrade gradually tends to stabilize. Frequency-domain analysis shows that the acceleration response is dominated by the excitation-frequency component together with smaller harmonic components, while the spectral amplitudes vary with the number of passes, reflecting changes in the nonlinear dynamic response during compaction. The degree of compaction results demonstrate that the compaction of the sandstone subgrade does not increase monotonically with the number of passes; instead, it first decreases and then increases as the number of passes increases. A comparison of different rolling speeds reveals that lower rolling speeds are more conducive to the transmission of vibratory energy into deeper layers, resulting in a more uniform and stable compaction effect. In contrast, higher rolling speeds generate larger instantaneous peak accelerations but lead to relatively insufficient compaction in deeper layers.</jats:p>
title: Dynamic response of large-thickness sandstone subgrade under strong vibratory compaction and optimization of construction parameters

items.abstract:
<jats:p>Islamic financial technology (FinTech) institutions increasingly rely on machine-learning systems whose opacity complicates Shari'a oversight, regulatory accountability and responsible innovation for strong institutions and sustainable, inclusive finance. Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) has been proposed as a remedy, yet its contribution to organizational digital maturity and to digital Shari'a governance in faith-based finance remains empirically untested. This study examines whether XAI techniques affect the digital maturity of Islamic FinTech institutions and their digital Shari'a governance and compliance, and whether professionals' perceptions differ across institutional maturity stages. It employs primary survey data from a purposive sample of 1,300 digital transformation managers, Shari'a supervisory board members and data analysts working in Islamic FinTech institutions, measured on a four-dimension, twelve-item Likert instrument (Cronbach's α = 0.74–0.91) and analysed with Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, ordinal logistic regression, simple linear regression and the Kruskal–Wallis test. The results show that XAI techniques exert a significant positive effect on digital Shari'a governance and compliance (β = 0.434, R2 = 0.216, F = 35.37, p < 0.001), whereas their effect on digital maturity is non-significant (B = 0.056, Wald = 0.044, p = 0.834) and perceptions do not differ across maturity levels (H = 0.606, p = 0.738). Descriptively, XAI and transparency (mean = 4.30) and infrastructure readiness (mean = 4.33) are rated very high, while governance and Shari'a compliance is rated high (mean = 3.81) and 55.4% of institutions self-classify as digital beginners. The findings suggest that algorithmic transparency functions as a targeted governance instrument that strengthens Shari'a accountability rather than as a general driver of digital maturity in Islamic FinTech.
JEL Classification Codes: G21, G28, O33, M15, Z12, C83.</jats:p>
title: Explainable artificial intelligence, digital maturity and shari'a compliance in islamic fintech: Evidence for responsible innovation and strong institutions

                    The primary objective of this study is to establish a collection of novel inequalities that extend and enhance existing mathematical inequality results. To this end, we introduce a new fuzzy fractional integral (
                    <jats:inline-formula id="j_dema-2025-0273_ineq_001">

                    <jats:inline-formula id="j_dema-2025-0273_ineq_002">

                      </jats:alternatives>
                    </jats:inline-formula>
                    ) convex mappings, referred to as
                    <jats:inline-formula id="j_dema-2025-0273_ineq_003">

                      </jats:alternatives>
                    </jats:inline-formula>
                    generalized strong
                    <jats:italic>h</jats:italic>
                    -convex mappings (
                    <jats:inline-formula id="j_dema-2025-0273_ineq_004">
                      <jats:alternatives>
                        <m:math xmlns:m="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll">

                            <m:mi mathvariant="script">F</m:mi>

                            <m:mi mathvariant="script">V</m:mi>
                            <m:mo>−</m:mo>

items.abstract: <jats:p>By employing macroscopic quantum electrodynamics (QED) and the Green tensor formalism, we describe the dynamics of a system composed of a quantum emitter (QE) radiating close to a two-dimensional graphene substrate. Due to the resonant coupling between the QE and the field of the surface plasmons (SPs) supported by the graphene substrate, it is possible for the system to transition from the weak-coupling regime, with Markovian dynamics, to the strong-coupling regime, in which the dynamics are non-Markovian. We pay special attention to the role of the geometrical and constitutive parameters in this transition, exploiting the tunability of the graphene plasmon dispersion relation to maintain the resonant conditions under such variations. In particular, we show the crossover from Markovian to non-Markovian behavior as the QE–graphene distance is reduced, with the chemical potential adjusted to maintain resonance. Furthermore, we study how the graphene losses—modeled through the carrier scattering rate—affect these regimes and, consequently, the system’s coherence. Our results provide a tunable platform for controlling strong light–matter interaction and non-Markovian dynamics in graphene-based plasmonic systems.</jats:p>
title: Electrostatic tuning of emitter–plasmon interactions for strong-coupling control

items.abstract:
<jats:p>
                    Metamorphic (de)volatilization reactions play fundamental roles in many geodynamic processes and are frequently associated with propagating reaction fronts, yet the mechanisms controlling front propagation remain poorly constrained. Here, we derive new analytical solutions for fluid pressure-driven (de)volatilization reaction fronts in porous rocks. The solutions predict that reaction-zone width increases with the square root of time, a scaling that arises from mass conservation across the moving reaction front rather than from classical hydraulic pore-pressure diffusion. Front propagation is governed by an effective diffusivity that depends on both hydraulic and chemical parameters, including reaction-induced density changes. Unlike conventional hydraulic diffusivity, which neglects reaction-induced density variations and generally predicts much faster propagation, the effective diffusivity captures the retardation of reaction fronts caused by density changes, with larger reaction-induced density changes producing slower propagation. In addition to a single-front formulation, we derive an analytical solution for two simultaneously propagating, coupled reaction fronts. The fronts are dynamically linked through mass conservation, preventing independent propagation and causing the leading front to advance faster than the trailing front. Both the single- and two-front solutions closely match numerical simulations. Application of the two-front model to published gypsum dehydration experiments shows that accounting for pore-water to pore-vapor transitions yields more realistic permeability estimates than single-front models. Application to natural metamorphic reactions predicts permeabilities between 10
                    <jats:sup>−18</jats:sup>
                    and 10
                    <jats:sup>−24</jats:sup>
                     m
                    <jats:sup>2</jats:sup>
                    , consistent with independent experimental, geophysical, and geological estimates. By analogy, the analytical framework can also be extended to chemically controlled reaction fronts governed solely by chemical diffusion. The analytical solutions provide a quantitative framework for estimating the timescales of natural and experimental (de)volatilization processes involving propagating reaction fronts.
                  </jats:p>
title: Beyond hydraulic diffusion: reaction front propagation and timescales in metamorphic (de)volatilization processes

items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Rapid, precise localization of gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) requires continuous wide-field imaging at hard X-ray and soft gamma-ray energies. We develop a fixed (nonrotating) modulation-collimator architecture to address this challenge. A bigrid collimator, a pair of aligned, periodic slit grids in front of a simple, nonimaging photon-counting detector, transmits an off-axis source through a triangular fringe pattern whose local angular position, the source phase, is recovered from simultaneous count rates in several grid pairs at fixed relative phase offsets, rather than by mechanically rotating a single grid pair as in the classical rotating modulation collimator (RMC). Four-phase demodulation of these count rates robustly cancels detector background and grid leakage without requiring rotation. Because the fringe pattern repeats across the sky, a phase measurement corresponds to many candidate source positions; we resolve this ambiguity over an arbitrarily wide field of view (FOV) using a cascade of grid stages with progressively longer beat periods (and pitches that converge toward a common finest value), generalizing the two-grid vernier-scale technique originally used to localize Sco X-1. This vernier cascade technique reduces the required photon counts and grid-calibration accuracy required to achieve fine angular resolution over a broad FOV. Generalized to two dimensions with orthogonal cascades, the resulting architecture achieves wide-field localization with no moving parts, no time modulation, and only simple photon-counting detectors, a promising candidate for simple, inexpensive, continuous-monitoring instruments supporting time-domain and multimessenger astrophysics.</jats:p>
title: Wide-field Localization Using Fixed Modulation Collimators

items.abstract: <jats:p>Depleted oil reservoirs considered for CO2 storage require an assessment of their coupled geomechanical response to injection, because production has altered their pore pressure and stress state. This study develops a probabilistic coupled flow–geomechanics framework and applies it to the Tenerife Field, a depleted, compartmentalized reservoir in Colombia’s Middle Magdalena Valley Basin. A history-matched black-oil model was converted to a coupled compositional model in CMG-GEM, and 330 Latin hypercube scenarios were generated by varying the cohesion and friction angle of the Mugrosa C lithologies and the annual CO2 injection profiles. The response was evaluated using the minimum Safety Factor (minSF) and maximum vertical displacement (maxDz) through empirical exceedance frequencies and Spearman correlations. In K30, the reservoir layer below the local seal, minSF ranged from 0.766 to 0.813 (median 0.779), and maxDz had a median of 0.193 ft and a P90 of 0.203 ft. No scenario reached the onset of shear yielding (minSF = 0). Injected CO2 volume showed the strongest association with both indicators, whereas cohesion and friction angle showed no significant association. These results apply only to the explored parameter space, do not constitute a safety certification, and do not evaluate the regional seal or fault reactivation.</jats:p>
title: Coupled Flow–Geomechanics Probabilistic Framework for Assessing CO2 Storage Integrity in a Depleted Colombian Oil Field: Application to the Tenerife Field

<jats:p>Radiation has always been present and is all around us. Life has evolved in a world containing
significant levels of ionizing radiation. Our bodies are adopted to it. Background exposure from
normal levels of the naturally occurring radioactive materials (NORMS) are present in all
environmental materials and do not vary remarkably from place to place. Where human activities
(Laboratory activities, pollution mining and others) have increased the relative concentration of
the radionuclides, they are referred to as the technologically enhanced naturally occurring
radioactive materials. Certain types of building materials are known to be radioactive. Exposure
to indoor ionizing radiation like exposure to any other type of ionizing radiation results in critical
health challenges. The aim of this research work is to determine the level of indoor and outdoor
ionizing radiation in some science laboratories in federal college of education, Yola, These science
laboratories usually harbour a number of active radiation sources. The ionizing radiation levels
were measured using gamma scout (model GS2 with serial number, for the data collection 20
readings were taking for indoor and outdoor and the data measured were read on the display
screen of the gamma-scout device. The gamma-scout hand held device was used obtained data for
the study was adjusted to detect the alpha, beta and gamma types of radiation in µSv/hr. The mean
equivalent dose rate per hour for indoor background ionizing radiation for the laboratories was
found to be 0.012mSv/hr while the outdoor was 0.084µSv/hr. The mean annual equivalent dose
rate of the laboratories ware compute for indoor and outdoor background radiation level to be
0.013mSv/yr and 0.22mSv/yr respectively, and it concluded that all the science laboratories in the
study are in a good proportion below the world wide average dose of 2.4mSv/yr.it was
recommended that periodic measurement of ionizing radiation level checking should be done all
doors and windows of laboratories are open daily in other to expel some accumulated redox gases.</jats:p>
title: Evaluation of Background Ionizing Radiation Level in Some Science Laboratories in Federal College of Education Yola

items.abstract: <jats:p>Geopolymers blended with silica fume (SF) offer enhanced performance, but the influence of the curing sequence on their properties remains unexplored. This study examines, for the first time, the impact of ambient curing (AC) prior to heat curing (HC) on the strength and reaction products of geopolymer mortars (GPMs) based on SF and fly ash (FA), highlighting their process–structure–property relationships. The initial AC periods were 0–48 h, while HC was conducted at 60°C for 48 h and 100°C for 24 h. Under optimal curing conditions, GPM30 with 5% SF achieved a compressive strength of 54 MPa after initial AC for 48 h and HC at 100°C for 24 h. This was an increase of 42% over GPM26 (5% SF), which reached only 37 MPa after direct HC for 24 h, highlighting the benefit of initial AC. X-ray diffraction and Rietveld analysis confirmed the presence of additional crystalline phases of albite, aragonite and anorthite minerals, indicating the formation of a stable, dense geopolymer matrix under optimal curing conditions. The retention of moisture, as indicated by Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy and attributed to the presence of SF, increased the curing efficiency. The results of this work highlight the correlation between curing, aluminosilicate structure and compressive strength, offering insights into optimising curing conditions for SF-blended FA-based geopolymers.</jats:p>
title: Influence of initial ambient curing on reaction products and strength development in fly ash–silica fume geopolymers

<jats:p>Single-aperture stellar kinematics jointly constrain the mass distribution, tracer light profile, and velocity anisotropy. Their coupling affects the interpretation of an inferred anisotropy.
We quantify how tracer-profile assumptions and data treatment affect common-anisotropy comparisons and inferred mass-density slopes in a compiled galaxy-scale lens sample.
We analyzed 107 lenses using distinct supernova counterparts, spatial flatness, distance duality, and the full supernova covariance. We compared the individual-slope power-law tracer with Hernquist and Sérsic profiles using measured effective radii. Numerical Jeans solutions, likelihood comparisons, posterior distributions, and controlled recovery experiments quantified the effects of tracer representation.
The power-law fixed-minus-free Bayesian information criterion differences are 6.74 for isotropy and 41.51 for fixed β=0.18, compared with -3.89 and -2.26 for Hernquist and -4.67 and -4.30 for Sérsic n=4. The preference also changes with the Sérsic index. Removing 12 systems with a linearized distance-ratio uncertainty of above 20% reduces the power-law isotropy comparison to 2.51. In isotropic Sérsic n=4 and Hernquist simulations, power-law fits yield Δ _0>6 in 60.0% and 50.0% of realizations, respectively, compared with 0.5% and 1.0% for matched-tracer fits. BIC
The preference for a common free anisotropy parameter depends on the tracer representation and sample composition. Controlled recovery identifies tracer mismatch as one mechanism that can generate this preference within the adopted aperture models. Physical interpretation requires a joint treatment of photometry, distance uncertainties, and kinematic weighting.</jats:p>
title: Anisotropy and tracer-profile assumptions in aperture-based strong-lens dynamics. Conditional inference from supernova distance ratios and unresolved stellar kinematics

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The development of polyurethanes combining high strength, excellent toughness, efficient self-healing, and recyclability remains challenging because of the inherent trade-off between network dynamics and cohesive energy. Soft segments in polyurethanes are generally regarded as flexible components that mainly govern chain mobility, whereas their role in regulating intermolecular organization has received much less attention. Varying the soft-segment ratio redistributes carbonyl-related hydrogen bonds and changes the local intermolecular interaction environment and nanoscale phase structure, leading to distinct chain relaxation behaviors. This coupled regulation of molecular structure and chain dynamics promotes molecular rearrangement while preserving sufficient reversible intermolecular interactions for effective interfacial load transfer. The resulting material achieved a self-healing efficiency of up to 97.65% after 12 h at 40 °C and an adhesion strength of 4.7 MPa on a copper substrate. All samples exhibited good thermal stability and repeatable processability. By tuning the relative proportions of the two soft segments to tailor molecular architecture and chain dynamics, this strategy modulates intermolecular interactions and local chain organization, providing valuable insights into the rational design of multifunctional self-healing polyurethanes.</jats:p>
title:
Synergistic Regulation of Molecular Structure and
Chain Dynamics through Soft-Segment Engineering Enables Efficient
Self-Healing and Strong Adhesion in Polyurethanes

<jats:p>The US-brokered peace agreement signed between Armenia and Azerbaijan on 8 August 2025 included a provision for constructing a transit route with US involvement. The route should connect Azerbaijan to its exclave of Nakhichevan through southern Armenia and will apparently follow the old railway along the Aras River on the border with Iran.

The agreement was covered negatively by the Iranian media and equated to the implementation of the so-called “Zangazur corridor”, with some officials sharply criticizing the construction of the route. For years, Iran had opposed this corridor, proposed after the 2020 Karabakh War, for multiple reasons. First, Iran feared the corridor would sever its land access to Armenia if the route did not remain under Yerevan's sovereignty. Second, Iran was wary of the creation of a "pan-Turkic" corridor, which would bring its northwestern frontier under the control of Turkey and Azerbaijan. And the third concern was the allies of these countries, namely Turkey’s membership in NATO and Azerbaijan’s close ties with Israel.

One theory that resurfaced in the Iranian media was that Reza Shah was to blame for the risks Iran faced from the “Zangazur corridor”. According to this theory, Reza Shah gave away the narrow strip of land connecting Turkey with Nakhichevan, and hence Azerbaijan.

The land concession in question dates to the 1932 Tehran Convention, under which the two countries swapped territories. However, the deal does not mention the sliver of territory connecting Turkey to Nakhichevan, as Turkey already controlled it and the 1921 Kars Treaty defined the border between Turkey and the Caucasus Soviet republics. Iran did consider this land its own. But Reza Shah decided to drop Iran’s claims during negotiations.</jats:p>
title: THE IRANIAN REACTION TO THE ARMENIA-AZERBAIJAN DEAL AND THE EFFECTS OF THE 1930S IRAN-TURKEY LAND SWAP

items.abstract: <jats:p>Due to the development of electric cars, portable electronic devices, and energy storage, lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) have experienced an increase in energy density demand. However, restrictions associated with the design of classical electrodes hinder the improvement of batteries' characteristics. The present review article examines three types of anode materials, namely, graphite, graphene, and silicon, as well as their distinct features. First, despite low cost and reliable cycling ability, the capacity of graphite is limited by 372 mAh g⁻¹. Second, high conductivity and lithium storage capacities are provided by graphene, but there is a possibility of aggregation of its sheets that can cause instability. Last but not least, silicon attracts special attention owing to its potential capacity of 3579 mAh g⁻¹. But the constant expansion of silicon makes it harmful for the structure of the electrode and solid electrolyte interphase. In order to resolve these issues, three modification approaches, i.e., structural engineering, composite with carbon materials, and modification of the interface, are proposed. Experimental data support positive outcomes related to the use of such modifications and improvement of the electrode capacity and performance. At last, the drawbacks of silicon-containing anodes, namely production difficulties, electrode swelling, and gap between the experiment and industrial practice, are discussed.</jats:p>
title: Challenges in Achieving High Energy Density in Lithium-Ion Batteries: Anode Materials and Silicon Modification Strategies

items.abstract: <jats:p>An old but recurring question in ground-state density functional theory, relevant to the construction of density functional approximations, is the existence of a second-order gradient expansion for the exchange energy that is exact for densities that vary slowly over space. Here, we will argue that there is such an expansion, with a gradient coefficient 10/7 of Sham’s, as suggested by theoretical/mathematical derivations and by numerical calculations on model slowly varying metallic densities, although some standard derivations do not quite capture the correct gradient coefficient. We also discuss long-range anomalies in the gradient expansions for the exchange and correlation holes around an electron. It is plausible that, as suggested earlier and recently, standard derivations are still correct for the coefficient of the second-order gradient expansion for exchange and correlation together, in which case the correct gradient coefficient for correlation is Cc=Cxc−Cx. We propose possible numerical evaluations of Cxc and Cx that are free from long-range anomalies, and discuss implications for density functional approximations. Axel Becke’s 1988 generalized gradient approximation (the B88 GGA) for the exchange energy brought density functional theory into chemistry, with a gradient coefficient for exchange that is optimal at the GGA level for atoms and molecules but too large for solids. Meta-GGAs seem to work as well for molecules as for solids, but may not be perfected yet. The article concludes with a few memories that the first author has of discussions with Axel Becke.</jats:p>
title: Is there a density-gradient expansion for the electronic exchange energy?

items.abstract: <jats:p>The 3D digitization of ancient architecture has long been constrained by large spatial-scale spans, heterogeneous precision levels, and inconsistent deliverable standards, with acquisition selection, fusion strategies, and modeling methods depending heavily on expert experience. This paper formalizes these experience-dependent procedures into computable decision models for intelligent multi-source heterogeneous 3D digitization. A three-level decision model is constructed with the target identifiable minimum feature size Rmin and precision levels as decision variables. At the perception level, a scale-aware sensor-selection model organizes six modalities into four complementary acquisition channels and back-calculates the operational parameters from Rmin. At the fusion level, a precision-level-aware three-layer architecture of “datum–skeleton–detail” and a five-component error-budget model establish an explicit and verifiable transfer from instrument precision to deliverable precision. At the construction level, a semantics-driven pipeline automatically produces PBR-LOD digital assets from the C1–C7 semantic categories. Ten ancient-architecture and immovable-relic scenes were used for validation. The horizontal and vertical mean errors of the fused models were 3.1 mm and 3.6 mm, satisfying the <10 mm requirement; the predicted total error (4.5 mm) agreed with the measured value within 1%; and 543 component assets with 8192 × 8192 PBR maps and three LOD levels were delivered with a naming-compliance rate of 100%. The method transforms heritage digitization from experience-dependent operations into reproducible and auditable digital-asset production.</jats:p>
title: Intelligent Decision-Making Method for Multi-Source Heterogeneous 3D Digitization of Ancient Architecture—An Integrated Technical System of Perception–Fusion–Construction–Delivery for High-Precision Digital Assets

Initial optimisation identifies breeder-to-multiplier volumetric ratios that maximise TBR at time zero, followed by time-dependent simulations to quantify TBR degradation due to lithium depletion during service. It is shown that while higher initial multiplier fractions enhance TBR, they also accelerate lithium depletion, reducing blanket lifetime. Conversely, hybrid ceramics with intrinsic neutron multiplication show reduced sensitivity to additional multipliers. Verification against FISPACT-II confirms the accuracy of the OpenMC depletion methodology utilised. The results highlight the importance of spatially optimised material distributions and lithium inventory management in maximising breeder blanket longevity. This work provides a robust framework for the design of next-generation solid breeder blankets, offering practical strategies to minimise replacement frequency and support sustainable fusion energy.

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    In this work, highly reinforced self-cleaning nanocomposites based on low-density polyethylene (LDPE), polyvinyl butyral (PVB), and bismuth oxide (Bi
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    O
                    <jats:sub>3</jats:sub>
                    ) nanoparticles were successfully fabricated using electron-beam (EB) irradiation. LDPE/PVB blends with varying PVB contents were prepared to improve matrix compatibility. Among the investigated compositions, the LDPE/PVB (95/5 wt%) blend exhibited the optimum properties and was subsequently reinforced with 3 parts per hundred resin (phr) Bi
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    O
                    <jats:sub>3</jats:sub>
                    nanoparticles to fabricate LDPE/PVB/Bi
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    O
                    <jats:sub>3</jats:sub>
                    nanocomposites. The LDPE/PVB (95/5 wt%) composition showed optimum performance. Reinforcement with 3 parts per hundred resin (phr) Bi
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    O
                    <jats:sub>3</jats:sub>
                    nanoparticles to fabricate LDPE/PVB/Bi
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    O
                    <jats:sub>3</jats:sub>
                    nanocomposites using a Brabender-like mixing apparatus and subsequent exposure to EB irradiation at different doses (10–150 kGy). Gel fraction and crosslink density calculations confirmed that EB irradiation up to 100 kGy provides the optimum dose, as radiation-induced crosslinking strengthens the polymer network and results in pronounced improvements in mechanical strength, thermal stability, and interfacial interaction. Comprehensive characterizations were performed using X-ray diffraction (XRD), Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR), scanning electron microscopy (SEM), transmission electron microscopy (TEM), thermogravimetric analysis (TGA), and contact angle measurements. The results confirmed homogeneous Bi
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    O
                    <jats:sub>3</jats:sub>
                    nanoparticle dispersion, enhanced structural integrity, and improved surface properties. The synergistic effect of PVB/Bi
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    O
                    <jats:sub>3</jats:sub>
                    incorporation into LDPE and EB irradiation markedly increased hydrophobicity, raising the water contact angle from 93° (neat LDPE) to 142° (irradiated nanocomposite). Furthermore, photocatalytic self-cleaning efficiency was significantly enhanced, achieving 94% methylene blue degradation under UV irradiation, compared to only 16% for neat LDPE. The kinetic analysis confirmed that the pseudo-first-order model provided superior correlation (R² = 0.985–0.998), establishing photocatalysis as the dominant degradation pathway. Overall, the developed LDPE/PVB/Bi
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    O
                    <jats:sub>3</jats:sub>
                    nanocomposites exhibited superior mechanical strength, thermal stability, hydrophobicity, and self-cleaning performance, demonstrating their potential for advanced packaging, environmental remediation, and outdoor engineering applications requiring durable multifunctional polymeric materials.
                  </jats:p>
