<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Monitor of All-Sky X-Ray Image (MAXI) has observed 144 gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) as of 2023 June; 76 reported through GCN Circulars and 68 only by MAXI. MAXI is more sensitive in the low-energy 2–20 keV band than most other GRB instruments, making it particularly suitable for detecting X-ray flashes (XRFs) and low-luminosity GRBs (LLGRBs). Here, we present a spectral and temporal study of 114 GRBs with reasonable statistics; accordingly, data for 65 and 49 events from the aforementioned categories (groups A and B, respectively) are analyzed. Our time-averaged spectral analyses of the group B events reveal diverse spectral properties, including soft and hard spectra at the low flux of ${\lt}10^{-8}$ erg cm$^{-2}$ s$^{-1}$. No clear positive correlation is found between flux and spectral hardness among them. For 17 events with soft spectra and sufficient photon statistics, we constrain the observer-frame peak energy, $E_{\mathrm{peak}}^{\mathrm{obs}}$. Assuming the Band function with the low-energy photon index fixed at $\alpha =-1.2$, we derive 90% confidence upper limits on $E_{\mathrm{peak}}^{\mathrm{obs}}$. These constraints are consistent with at least some of the soft MAXI/GSC events having lower $E_{\mathrm{peak}}^{\mathrm{obs}}$ than typical GRBs. The soft and faint group B events may therefore include intrinsically soft XRF-like events or GRBs whose spectra are shifted to lower $E_{\mathrm{peak}}^{\mathrm{obs}}$ by cosmological redshift. The group B sample also contains relatively hard events, which could be interpreted as high-redshift GRBs or nearby LLGRBs such as GRB 170817A. We further investigate the spectral softness using the flux ratio $F_{2-8\, \mathrm{keV}}/F_{8-20\, \mathrm{keV}}$. Adopting a boundary of 0.96 for the 2–20 keV band, 30 of the 82 “simul” and group B events are classified as soft GRBs, while 52 are classified as classical-GRB candidates. Furthermore, the logN–logS distribution suggests many group B events may be nearby GRBs. Consequently, the group B events are plausible candidates for nearby LLGRBs and/or XRFs.</jats:p>
title: MAXI sample of gamma-ray bursts possibly favors low-luminosity ones and X-ray flashes

<jats:p>
                    We describe an all-electron implementation of the Bethe–Salpeter equation (BSE) for the calculation of optical absorption spectra in the full-potential linearized augmented-plane-wave (FLAPW) method. So far, FLAPW implementations have resorted to a simple plane-wave basis for the bare and screened Coulomb potentials, thereby forgoing the all-electron description to some extent. In contrast, we expand the interaction potentials in the all-electron mixed basis. The Coulomb divergence is treated analytically, allowing for anisotropic screening. As in most implementations, the BSE is solved by the diagonalization of a two-particle Hamiltonian matrix, whose dimension is proportional to the number of
                    <a:math xmlns:a="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML">
                      <a:mi mathvariant="bold">k</a:mi>
                    </a:math>
                    points. Because of the large number of
                    <c:math xmlns:c="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML">
                      <c:mi mathvariant="bold">k</c:mi>
                    </c:math>
                    points required to converge the BSE, the resulting matrix becomes large even for small unit cells. We describe a method that exploits the crystal symmetries to accelerate the construction and diagonalization of the two-particle Hamiltonian. In particular, we employ group-theoretical tools to bring the Hamiltonian into block-diagonal form. Furthermore, it is shown that often only one of the blocks needs to be taken into account for the optical absorption spectrum, leading to a considerable speedup of the diagonalization step. The code allows for the inclusion of spin–orbit coupling and is parallelized with the possibility of storing the Hamiltonian in distributed memory over many nodes, keeping the memory demand on a single node low. To validate our implementation, we show optical absorption spectra and report exciton binding energies for bulk Si, LiF, and
                    <e:math xmlns:e="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML">
                      <e:msub>
                        <e:mi>MoS</e:mi>
                        <e:mn>2</e:mn>
                      </e:msub>
                    </e:math>
                    . By exploiting the crystal symmetries, we can reduce the dimension of the Hamiltonian matrix of Si by a factor of five, resulting in a theoretical 125-fold speedup for the leading cubic scaling term of the diagonalization. The calculated spectra agree with available theoretical and experimental spectra from the literature. The calculated exciton binding energies of 22 meV and 76 meV for Si and
                    <f:math xmlns:f="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML">
                      <f:msub>
                        <f:mi>MoS</f:mi>
                        <f:mn>2</f:mn>
                      </f:msub>
                    </f:math>
                    are closer to experimental values than in previous BSE studies.
                  </jats:p>
title: Efficient all-electron Bethe-Salpeter implementation using crystal symmetries

<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>This study presents semi‐analytical investigation of the coupled transport of momentum, heat, and pollutant concentration in a porous ground surface, incorporating advective, diffusive, and reactive mechanisms. Unlike conventional analytical approaches that often neglect coupling effects or rely purely on numerical approximations, the present model integrates the incompressible Navier‐Stokes equations with nonlinear heat transfer and advection‐diffusion‐reaction formulations to capture the multiphysics nature of subsurface transport processes. Using Lie symmetry analysis, the governing nonlinear system of partial differential equations is reduced to ordinary differential equations, which are then solved using a perturbation‐based approach that linearises the system into a solvable set of linear equations, allowing direct integration under defined validity conditions. The combined use of Lie symmetry analysis and the perturbation method is adopted because the reduced equations remain strongly coupled and nonlinear, and therefore do not readily admit solutions through standard special‐function or Green's function techniques, while still preserving explicit dependence on the governing physical parameters. Parametric analysis shows that increased decay reduces pollutant penetration depth, higher Reynolds numbers enhance advective dominance and steepen concentration gradients, and thermal effects influence velocity profiles and contaminant dispersion. These findings provide additional physical insights into the interplay among flow, heat, and reactive transport in porous media, offering a simpler, more reproducible integration framework for predicting pollutant fate. The proposed model has practical relevance in groundwater contamination assessment and environmental remediation planning, particularly in scenarios where rapid yet reliable analytical approximations are required.</jats:p>
title: Analysis of Source‐to‐Sink Pollutant Transport in Porous Surface Using Lie Symmetry and Perturbation Method

items.abstract: <jats:p>Ingredient disclosure frameworks for personal care products (PCPs) do not capture impurities. We tested the purported link between diethylamino hydroxybenzoyl hexyl benzoate (DHHB), a common ultraviolet (UV) filter, and the presence of di-n-hexyl phthalate (DnHxP) as an impurity. Twenty-seven PCPs containing DHHB and controls (PCPs without DHHB) were analyzed using gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GC-MS), targeting 15 phthalates. DnHxP was detected in 44% of products containing DHHB and was below detection in controls. Levels suggest that a subset of DHHB-containing PCPs on the European market would face compliance problems once 10 ppm limits on the presence of DnHxP as an impurity in DHHB come into force. These findings highlight impurities as a plausible and underrecognized source of exposure to restricted phthalates from PCPs, and indicate that improved transparency and impurity control are needed to ensure compliance with the Cosmetics Regulation (EC No. 1223/2009) and safe PCPs.</jats:p>
title: Phthalate impurities in UV filters as an underrecognized source of exposure: evidence from European sunscreens and other personal care products

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Mechanical deformation and thermal variation provide complementary information for interpreting tactile interactions and physiological activity at the skin interface. This study presents a tactile sensing platform that couples polyvinylidene fluoride-co-trifluoroethylene-based multifunctional epidermal electronics with a synchronous interface module for simultaneous acquisition of mechanical and thermal signals. The multifunctional epidermal electronics use a piezoelectric film as both the flexible substrate and active layer, integrating a central piezoelectric pressure sensor with a surrounding Al serpentine resistance temperature detector. Separate electrodes and electrical paths preserve independent sensing outputs while maintaining a compact and flexible device architecture suitable for conformal attachment to curved biological surfaces without requiring additional supporting substrates. The synchronous interface module incorporates dedicated analog front ends, electrical isolation, signal-appropriate sampling, channel-specific filtering, and synchronized digitization on a common time axis, enabling reliable comparison of signals with distinct electrical and temporal characteristics. Device characterization established stable piezoelectric pressure sensing, reproducible thermoresistive behavior, and quantitative bounds on bending-induced resistance modulation. Sustained and brief fingertip contacts produced distinguishable mechanical event patterns and thermal accumulation and recovery behaviors, demonstrating the complementary temporal information provided by the two sensing modalities. In small-animal measurements, the platform simultaneously tracked respiration-induced mechanical deformation and skin temperature changes associated with anesthesia and recovery. Human measurements further demonstrated concurrent acquisition of arterial pulse waveforms and local skin temperature at multiple body sites, revealing location-dependent physiological characteristics. By integrating structurally compact multifunctional epidermal electronics with signal-specific synchronous instrumentation, this platform provides a unified approach for resolving fast mechanical events and slower thermal variations within the same attachment area. The proposed architecture supports tactile sensing and physiological monitoring while offering a practical framework for flexible multimodal bioelectronic systems.</jats:p>
title: Multifunctional epidermal electronics-based tactile sensing platform coupled with synchronous interface module

items.abstract: <jats:p>The 3D digitization of ancient architecture has long been constrained by large spatial-scale spans, heterogeneous precision levels, and inconsistent deliverable standards, with acquisition selection, fusion strategies, and modeling methods depending heavily on expert experience. This paper formalizes these experience-dependent procedures into computable decision models for intelligent multi-source heterogeneous 3D digitization. A three-level decision model is constructed with the target identifiable minimum feature size Rmin and precision levels as decision variables. At the perception level, a scale-aware sensor-selection model organizes six modalities into four complementary acquisition channels and back-calculates the operational parameters from Rmin. At the fusion level, a precision-level-aware three-layer architecture of “datum–skeleton–detail” and a five-component error-budget model establish an explicit and verifiable transfer from instrument precision to deliverable precision. At the construction level, a semantics-driven pipeline automatically produces PBR-LOD digital assets from the C1–C7 semantic categories. Ten ancient-architecture and immovable-relic scenes were used for validation. The horizontal and vertical mean errors of the fused models were 3.1 mm and 3.6 mm, satisfying the <10 mm requirement; the predicted total error (4.5 mm) agreed with the measured value within 1%; and 543 component assets with 8192 × 8192 PBR maps and three LOD levels were delivered with a naming-compliance rate of 100%. The method transforms heritage digitization from experience-dependent operations into reproducible and auditable digital-asset production.</jats:p>
title: Intelligent Decision-Making Method for Multi-Source Heterogeneous 3D Digitization of Ancient Architecture—An Integrated Technical System of Perception–Fusion–Construction–Delivery for High-Precision Digital Assets

items.abstract:
<jats:sec id="background">
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>In mechanically ventilated children with critical asthma, increasing minute ventilation can improve carbon dioxide clearance but may shorten expiratory time and worsen gas trapping, intrinsic positive end-expiratory pressure (auto-PEEP), airway-pressure exposure, and hemodynamic burden. Because invasive ventilation is uncommon, respiratory therapists and other critical-care learners have limited opportunities to observe these trade-offs at the bedside.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec id="methods">
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We developed an open-source, computer-based mechanical ventilation simulator for teaching the physiological consequences of ventilator adjustments in pediatric critical asthma. Internal verification included automated physiological-direction checks, a same-patient respiratory-rate sweep, predefined teaching scenarios, one-at-a-time sensitivity analyses, and reproducibility testing. No patient data were used for clinical validation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec id="results">
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>In a fixed virtual patient with severe airflow obstruction, the simulated PaCO2 response improved as respiratory rate increased to approximately 22 breaths/min and then worsened at higher rates as expiratory time shortened. Auto-PEEP and plateau pressure increased progressively, while the mean arterial pressure surrogate declined at higher rates. Teaching scenarios and sensitivity analyses showed the expected directional behaviour.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec id="discussion">
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The simulator makes clinically relevant ventilatory trade-offs visible while keeping its assumptions open to inspection. The direction of the principal responses is consistent with established obstructive physiology, but absolute values and numerical thresholds remain educational surrogates rather than patient predictions.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec id="conclusion">
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This internally verified simulator provides a faculty-guided environment for teaching ventilatory trade-offs in pediatric critical asthma. It is an educational tool and has not been clinically validated against patient data.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Development and internal verification of an open-source mechanical ventilation simulator for teaching ventilatory trade-offs in pediatric critical asthma: A respiratory-care education tool

items.abstract: <jats:p>A central challenge in high-gain phototransistors is achieving strong photomultiplication while suppressing dark leakage. However, how interfacial traps regulate photoinduced carrier injection to achieve this balance remains insufficiently understood. Here, we employ technology computer-aided design (TCAD) simulations to investigate a vertical phototransistor (VPT) featuring an encapsulated-source architecture and a trap-assisted inorganic/organic heterojunction, with p-type NiO and polyfluorene serving as model inorganic and organic semiconductors, respectively. With suitable energy-level alignment at the heterojunction, the device exhibits distinct gate-dependent conduction regimes governed by trap-induced electrostatic modulation. In the OFF state, trapping of photogenerated electrons sustains negative interfacial charge and extends the electrostatic modulation beneath the encapsulated source. This modulation broadens the effective lateral hole-injection region near the source edge, rather than primarily narrowing the local vertical injection barrier, thereby enhancing zero-gate-bias photocurrent while maintaining ultralow dark leakage. In the ON state, the electrostatic modulation extends into the SC2 bulk, promoting a more uniform electrostatic potential distribution to facilitate hole transport and vertical injection for photomultiplication. Under the specified illumination and bias conditions, the design with a trap density of 1019 cm−3 exhibits the highest performance among the investigated cases, achieving a detectivity of 4.24 × 1013 Jones at zero gate bias, together with an ON-state external quantum efficiency of 31,790% and a responsivity of 110.25 A W−1. Structural analysis further shows that sufficiently thin source encapsulation preserves the OFF-state photoinduced conduction pathway while maintaining ON-state vertical carrier injection, enabling low-leakage optical sensing and high-gain photomultiplication. These findings highlight the complementary roles of interfacial trap engineering and source encapsulation in spatially regulating carrier injection, providing physical insights and design guidelines for high-gain, low-power, and highly sensitive VPTs.</jats:p>
title: Trap-Assisted Photomultiplication and Spatial Carrier Regulation in Encapsulated-Source Hybrid Vertical Phototransistors

<jats:p>
                    Stable carbon isotopes are often used to infer dominant methanogenic pathways in wetland ecosystems. We performed closed system incubations with
                    <jats:italic>Sphagnum</jats:italic>
                    bog peat, monitoring CO
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    and CH
                    <jats:sub>4</jats:sub>
                    production and isotopic composition across incubation temperatures and over time. We observed higher CO
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    production relative to CH
                    <jats:sub>4</jats:sub>
                    production (CO
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    /CH
                    <jats:sub>4</jats:sub>
                     > 1). Whereas for closed methanogenic systems one would typically expect the CO
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    pool and resultant CH
                    <jats:sub>4</jats:sub>
                    to become increasingly enriched as
                    <jats:sup>13</jats:sup>
                    C-depleted carbon is transformed to CH
                    <jats:sub>4</jats:sub>
                    , we saw the stable carbon isotopic composition of both gases became increasingly
                    <jats:sup>13</jats:sup>
                    C-depleted in parallel over the course of the incubations. We hypothesized that these unusual trends were due to CO
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    with organic matter isotopic composition (‑25 ‰) being added by non-fractionating catabolic processes at a higher rate than CO
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    reduction to CH
                    <jats:sub>4</jats:sub>
                    , resulting in increasing
                    <jats:sup>13</jats:sup>
                    C depletion in the CO
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    pool over time. Methane was formed from that increasingly depleted CO
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    pool at a relatively constant apparent fractionation factor and thus its δ
                    <jats:sup>13</jats:sup>
                    C became more depleted over time as well. We developed an explanatory mass balance model which reproduced our observations and was consistent with our hypothesis. The isotope mass balance model accurately reproduced changes in δ
                    <jats:sup>13</jats:sup>
                    C-CO
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    and δ
                    <jats:sup>13</jats:sup>
                    C-CH
                    <jats:sub>4</jats:sub>
                    under conditions consistent with hydrogenotrophic methanogenesis drawing from a progressively
                    <jats:sup>13</jats:sup>
                    C-depleted CO
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    pool. These results show the CO
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    /CH
                    <jats:sub>4</jats:sub>
                    production ratio strongly influences δ
                    <jats:sup>13</jats:sup>
                    C-CH
                    <jats:sub>4</jats:sub>
                    by controlling the δ
                    <jats:sup>13</jats:sup>
                    C-CO
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    . Small shifts in CO
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    -dominated versus CH
                    <jats:sub>4</jats:sub>
                    -dominated metabolism can substantially alter δ
                    <jats:sup>13</jats:sup>
                    C-CH
                    <jats:sub>4</jats:sub>
                    even in the absence of major changes in methanogenic pathway, potentially leading to misinterpretation of isotope signals from incubations, porewaters, or emissions if not considered.
                  </jats:p>
title: Influence of CO2/CH4 production ratios on the isotope signature of methane

items.abstract: <jats:p>Food security under changing climatic conditions requires attention to the connections between agricultural production, the preservation and movement of food, and people’s ability to obtain an adequate diet. Improvements in one part of this system do not necessarily produce improvements in the others. Additional production may be lost during storage and transport, while reliable supplies may remain economically inaccessible to particular communities. This article presents the rationale for three connected professional forums addressing soil, water and agricultural production; food storage and cold chains; and food security and supply systems. The forums are conceived as successive opportunities to examine a shared practical problem from different professional perspectives. Particular attention is given to local environmental conditions, infrastructure dependencies, limited access to expertise, and the feasibility of proposed measures. The Laboratory of Climate Change and Food Security provides an organisational framework for preparatory analysis, international expert participation, publications and subsequent collaborative work. The purpose is to connect scientific understanding with decisions that producers, businesses, public authorities and communities can implement and assess.</jats:p>
title: Climate Change and Food Security: Connecting Production, Preservation and Access

items.abstract: <jats:p>Brazzein is a compact, disulfide-rich sweet protein whose manufacturing value depends on the recovery of a precisely processed and functionally active product rather than on expression titre alone. This review integrates evidence on structure-sweetness relationships, recombinant hosts, fusion-assisted recovery, process stability, safety, and the use of spent brewer's yeast as a circular input. Yeast and fungal systems now reach high reported titres, while soluble fusion and engineered-aggregation routes provide distinct solutions to intracellular recovery. However, studies quantify different constructs and fractions, and analytical evidence of mass or folding does not by itself demonstrate sweetness. A six-stage evaluation framework is proposed that begins with a fixed product specification and compares host performance, primary recovery, cleavage, purification, functional activity, process retention, and circular-resource burden within one mass balance. The preferred endpoint is sequence-verified, tag-free, functionally active Brazzein recovered per litre of culture after a defined treatment. Applying this endpoint would enable fair head-to-head comparison of production routes and connect molecular engineering to food performance, techno-economics, and life-cycle assessment.</jats:p>
title: Active Recovery and Stability Engineering of Brazzein for Sustainable Production

items.abstract: <jats:p>Industrial development has expanded the availability of essential products, materials, medicines, and technologies. However, conventional chemical manufacturing can also generate hazardous waste and emissions, consume substantial energy and water, and intensify pressure on non-renewable resources. Green chemistry offers a preventive approach by designing chemical products and processes that reduce or eliminate hazardous substances at source. This review examines the contribution of green chemistry to cleaner production and sustainable industrial development, with particular attention to its core principles and selected developments in safer solvents, green synthesis, catalysis, renewable feedstocks, waste valorisation, and water-related technologies. It also considers environmental and economic implications, barriers to industrial implementation, and priorities for future research. The literature suggests that green chemistry can improve resource efficiency and reduce waste when environmental considerations are incorporated into process design rather than addressed only after production. These benefits, however, are not automatic: proposed alternatives need to be evaluated across their life cycles and under realistic operating conditions. Financial constraints, technical performance, regulatory requirements, and the challenge of scaling laboratory methods remain significant barriers. The review argues that progress depends on coordinated research, industrial investment, education, and transparent life-cycle-based evaluation.</jats:p>
title: Green Chemistry for Cleaner Production and Sustainable Industrial Development: A Critical Review

items.abstract:
<jats:p>Background: Stem cells’ ability to differentiate into other cell types makes them unique. Physical activity may influence stem cell production and mobilisation, but evidence across different age groups and exercise types remains fragmented.
Objectives: This review examined the relationship between physical activity and stem cell production in children, young adults and the elderly.
Method: Relevant articles were searched in Google Scholar, EBSCOhost Cumulative Index to Nursing and Allied Health Literature (CINAHL), PubMed and Web of Science. Following article selection, methodological quality assessment and data extraction, 19 articles were included. Risk of bias was assessed using Cochrane Collaboration and ROBINS-I tools, while evidence quality was evaluated using the GRADE system.
Results: Increased physical activity was associated with increased stem cell production and mobilisation in children, adults and the elderly. This relationship was observed with both aerobic and anaerobic exercise and appeared independent of stem cell type. Endurance and resistance exercise were associated with increases through different physiological and adaptive mechanisms.
Conclusion: Regular physical activity, whether endurance or resistance training, enhances stem cell production and mobilisation across the lifespan, highlighting its potential benefits for tissue repair, functional capacity, health and well-being.
Clinical Implications: Physiotherapists can prescribe targeted aerobic and resistance programmes based on frequency, intensity, time and type principles to stimulate endogenous stem cell activity and support muscle repair. For older adults, progressively loaded, higher-intensity and longer-duration exercise may maximise functional outcomes, although regenerative responses may be attenuated by age-related changes. These findings support exercise-based strategies for promoting healthy ageing and contribute to the United Nations Sustainable Development Goal 3.</jats:p>
title: Relationship between physical activity and stem cell production: A systematic review

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>This study investigates the vowel-length contrast in Seoul Korean (SK) and North Kyungsang Korean (NKK), integrating production and perception evidence to assess the state of sound change in the two varieties. In SK productions, only older women retain a durational contrast, while older men and all younger SK speakers show no detectable contrast. Older NKK speakers also maintain a robust durational contrast, but younger male NKK speakers exhibit a reduced contrast and younger women have none detectable. However, among NKK speakers, accentual categories are largely preserved; acoustic analysis of F0 shows that pitch differences between long- and short-vowel words are mediated by lexical accent category. Perception results diverge from production patterns, with NKK listeners showing higher identification accuracy than SK. When vowel duration and pitch-accent cues are placed in conflict, younger NKK listeners resolve the conflict in favor of pitch accent. These findings indicate a group-level production–perception dissociation and locate the source in perception. Because duration and pitch accent are lexically bundled in NKK, F0 is not an available dimension onto which the contrast can be reweighted. The change across generations is in the weight listeners assign to an already contrastive accentual cue as the secondary durational cue is lost.</jats:p>
title: Vowel-length merger in Korean according to variety, age, and gender: integrating production and perception evidence

<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Operations and supply chain managers are continuously pulled between efficiency to reduce costs and buffering for resilience. These endeavors are at the heart of Factory Physics, which theoretically defines the levers managers use to control the physics of an organization. However, organizations are also under pressure to incorporate environmental impacts into their decision-making due to consumer and regulatory pressures. With managerial decisions on inventory turnover and capacity utilization having direct environmental impacts, managers are thus challenged to consider environmental performance alongside economic consequences in an increasingly demanding environment. Taking a Factory Physics lens, this research focuses on the environmental impact of inventory turnover and capacity utilization, while considering potential nonlinearities.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A high-dimensional fixed-effects approach is employed with a panel dataset of 4,638 operations and supply chain firms from 2002 to 2026.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The results suggest that increasing inventory turnover and capacity utilization improve environmental performance. However, there is a nonlinearity: beyond a certain point, additional inventory turnover no longer improves environmental performance. A similar effect is found for capacity utilization when financial leverage is high. Extending this in a post hoc analysis, the findings suggest that capacity utilization is dominant in reducing environmental harm. Further, increasing inventory turnover only improves environmental performance in later stages of the process.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This research provides a holistic examination of the environmental implications of Factory Physics, considering the multiple levers managers use to manage Factory Physics and the potential for nonlinear outcomes.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Too lean? Exploring the nonlinear environmental implications of Factory Physics

<jats:p>
                    Biomass supports grid stability because, unlike wind and solar, it can be dispatched and stored on demand. Yet mid-term forecasts of biomass electricity generation remain scarce, particularly for national systems with limited installed capacity such as Greece. This study compares univariate SARIMA and exogenous SARIMAX models for monthly biomass electricity generation in Greece over 2014–2026, testing deterministic against stochastic seasonality and the role of installed capacity as an exogenous regressor. A SARIMA(0,1,1)(0,1,1)
                    <jats:sub>12</jats:sub>
                    model outperforms deterministic alternatives in short-term forecasts, while adding installed capacity in a SARIMAX(1,0,0)(0,1,1)
                    <jats:sub>12</jats:sub>
                    improves accuracy over the extended horizon, reflecting a cointegrating long-run relationship between capacity and output. An ex-post adjustment for zero-price hours and mandatory renewable energy curtailment suggests that recent regulatory shifts can also be captured within the SARIMAX framework, further improving forecast accuracy. These findings underline the value of combining technical and regulatory information in forecasting for grid operators and policymakers.
                  </jats:p>
title: Forecasting biomass electricity production in Greece with SARIMA and SARIMAX models – A methodological approach

items.abstract: <jats:p>Accurate pest detection supports crop monitoring and plant protection in chili pepper production. Small targets, scale variation, and complex vegetation backgrounds remain challenging. This study develops RAS-YOLO by integrating a RepViT backbone, an asymptotic feature pyramid network (AFPN), and a lightweight shared detail-enhanced convolutional detection head (LSDECD) into YOLO11n. Twenty-three configurations are investigated, comprising seven YOLO detectors, three backbone replacements, four feature-fusion alternatives, six detection-head alternatives, and three non-YOLO detectors. Following a data leakage examination, 59 overlapping images were excluded from the evaluation subsets, resulting in a dataset of 4935 images. RAS-YOLO was then evaluated on the corrected independent test set. RAS-YOLO achieved precision, recall, mAP50, and mAP50-95 values of 70.18%, 70.73%, 70.37%, and 30.89%, respectively. Relative to YOLO11n, precision and mAP50 increased by 8.52 and 1.72 percentage points, whereas recall and mAP50-95 decreased by 2.23 and 0.23 percentage points.LSDECD yields the highest precision and mAP50 among six replacement heads. The final model contains 6.51 million parameters, requires 22.01 GFLOPs, and reaches 113.2 frames per second in batch-one forward inference on an RTX 3090 GPU. A graphical interface demonstrates model integration and single-image detection. The results indicate a precision-oriented performance advantage accompanied by increased computational demand and reduced recall and strict-IoU accuracy relative to selected alternatives. Further evaluation is required to establish generalization across cultivation environments and practical field performance.</jats:p>
title: RAS-YOLO: Multiscale Visual Detection of Chili Pepper Diseases and Pests for Crop Production Monitoring

<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Drawing on the emotions-as-frames model (EFM), this study aims to examine the interaction between emotional framing and visual imagery in carbon pricing persuasion, focusing on the mediating role of message elaboration.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study used a 2 × 2 between-subjects experimental design (emotion: hope vs fear; visual image: present vs absent) with a sample of 300 participants. Data were analyzed using analysis of variance (ANOVA) and analysis of covariance (ANCOVA) to test for main and interaction effects while controlling for climate change knowledge. The PROCESS macro was used to test for mediation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The results indicated that fear framing was more persuasive than hope framing for behavioral intentions. The presence of a visual image in a fear-framed message showed a significant main effect on attitudes toward the climate change message. Furthermore, significant interaction was found between hope-framed messaging and visual imagery for attitudes toward the climate change message. Message elaboration, through evaluative processing, mediated the relationship between the emotional frames and the outcome variables. These effects remained robust after controlling for climate change knowledge.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Practical implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study offers important contributions and provides a messaging framework for policy practitioners and communication specialists, suggesting that emphasizing risks through fear-framed messages paired with relevant visuals is most effective for driving behavioral intentions for carbon pricing.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study advances the EFM by examining the interaction between emotion and a visual image, while accounting for the mediating role of message elaboration and the stability of these effects across varying levels of climate change knowledge.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Emotional framing and visual image in carbon pricing persuasion: the mediating role of message elaboration

<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Introduction</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Handmade cultural products derive value not only from how they are made but also from what consumers understand them to mean. This study examines how production visibility and cultural framing make different bases of worth available in consumer evaluation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A sequential mixed-methods design combined deductive specification, qualitative theory elaboration, and experimental testing. Study 1 combined 20 semi-structured interviews with fieldwork and observation in Chinese art-market settings to elaborate literature-derived pathways and identify an additional relational judgment concerning the connection between making and meaning. Study 2 tested the resulting framework in a 2 × 2 online experiment with 480 Chinese participants (120 per condition), following a separate stimulus pretest.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Production visibility increased perceived effort and handmade authenticity, whereas cultural framing primarily increased perceived cultural value. The joint presentation of production and cultural cues produced a significant interactive effect on purchase intention. Although both cues increased perceived process-meaning fit, their interaction did not, and process-meaning fit did not significantly mediate their interactive effect on purchase intention. As a secondary monetary outcome, willingness to pay showed positive main effects of both cues but no interaction.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The findings distinguish an evidential route through which visible production makes human labor and handmade origin available for inference from an interpretive route through which cultural framing makes product meaning intelligible. They further indicate that making multiple evaluative resources available does not necessarily mean that consumers integrate them into a coherent relational judgment.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Seeing the handmade: production visibility, cultural framing, and consumer valuation of handmade cultural products

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The growing body of literature on the data economy has focused almost exclusively on consumer data, whose provision is constrained by privacy costs. This paper broadens the scope by introducing two new data types: producer data, which are generated from economic production; and natural data, which can be either collected from nature directly or generated through scientific experiments. We develop a generalized semi‐endogenous growth model that includes all three types of data in a unified framework. Producer data carry no privacy externality, and the provision of these data scales endogenously with output, creating a self‐reinforcing feedback loop between production and innovation. Natural data share the absence of privacy costs but lack this feedback channel, isolating the growth contribution of each property. With the rapid advance of artificial intelligence, synthetic data, a special case of natural data in our framework, may substantially raise the efficiency of data generation, which raises the level of output. If this efficiency keeps improving over time, natural data can also narrow or even reverse the growth‐rate gap with producer data. The three types are combined through a constant elasticity of substitution  (CES) aggregator. Their elasticity of substitution acts as a structural switch: as it rises, the economy evolves from a consumer‐data‐dominated stage with relatively low growth to a producer‐data‐dominated stage with higher growth, which describes how the data economy transforms across development stages.</jats:p>
title: From consumption to production: a generalized model of growth for the data economy

items.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This paper aims to clarify the role of financial actors in sustainability transitions by developing and applying an archetype framework of financial agency logics. In transition studies, finance is often treated as a resource that flows towards promising innovations, rather than as a domain of agency shaping sustainability-related decision-making.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The paper adopts an abductive qualitative research design. An archetype framework is developed through engagement with sustainability transition theory and sustainable finance literature, and empirically explored through 13 semi-structured interviews with financial actors involved in Norwegian salmon farming production, complemented by 55 documents, including annual reports, sustainability strategies, investment guidelines and policy-related documents.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The findings reveal a misalignment between sustainability ambitions articulated in strategies and the logics guiding investment practices. While sustainability is commonly framed in line with sustainable logics, decision-making remains dominated by conventional orientations prioritising short-term profitability and narrowly defined risk. Transformative logics appear mainly in discursive commitments. Financial actors selectively mobilise overlapping logics depending on context, rather than conforming to a single archetype.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research limitations/implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study is limited to a single sector and national context. Future research should test and refine the framework across sectors and geographies and examine how financial instruments and policy mixes shape the mobilisation of financial logics.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Practical implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The framework offers a diagnostic lens for practitioners and policymakers to examine how sustainability ambitions are interpreted and filtered within financial decision-making.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The paper introduces a novel archetype framework that operationalises financial agency in sustainability transitions, responding to a call for more knowledge on the role of finance.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Between sustainability strategy and financial practice: archetypes of financial agency in Norwegian salmon farming

items.abstract: <jats:p>Arsenic (As) contamination of agricultural soils is an increasingly important constraint on the sustainability of plantation cropping systems, particularly tea (Camellia sinensis), coffee (Coffea spp.), rubber (Hevea brasiliensis), cocoa (Theobroma cacao), and perennial spice and fruit crops. Although arsenic occurs naturally in many soils, its accumulation is often intensified by geogenic enrichment, contaminated irrigation water, mining and industrial deposition, and historical use of arsenical pesticides and phosphate fertilizers. In plantation systems, long cropping cycles, permanent root systems, repeated agrochemical use, and dependence on shallow groundwater can promote gradual arsenic loading and exposure. Arsenic reduces plantation productivity by inhibiting root development, disrupting the uptake of water and nutrients, degrading chlorophyll and photosynthetic machinery, generating reactive oxygen species and altering carbon assimilation and hormone signalling. These effects can lower vegetative growth, reduce leaf, bean, latex, or fruit yields, and compromise produce quality and market acceptance. The severity of the impact depends on arsenic speciation, soil pH, redox status, iron and aluminium oxides, organic matter, microbial activity, and crop genotype. Tea is particularly relevant because acidic plantation soils, high root-zone exposure, and repeated leaf harvesting create conditions in which arsenic can accumulate in foliage; studies report arsenic partitioning predominantly in roots, with lower but measurable transfer to leaves. Management should therefore combine source control, irrigation-water testing, site-specific soil monitoring, avoidance of unnecessary phosphate inputs, iron- and silicon-based immobilization where appropriate, organic amendments, tolerant or low-accumulating planting material, and phytoremediation in severely affected areas. This review synthesizes current evidence on arsenic sources, soil–plant dynamics, physiological effects, plantation-crop responses, food-safety implications, and practical mitigation strategies. It concludes that plantation systems require long-term, landscape-scale monitoring and integrated management rather than single-point remediation.</jats:p>
title: Arsenic Contamination of Soil and Its Impact on Plantation Crop Production

<jats:p>This research aimed to empirically evaluate the surface and ground water quality of river Chochi
for sustainable food production. The study targeted river Chochi in Yola South LGA, of Adamawa
state. Along the river three (3) locations were selected where irrigation activities are intensively
carried out namely Bole, Modire and Anguwa-Tabo respectively. At each of the location three
samples of water were collected for both surface (river flowing water) and ground water (borehole
water) in three periods of the season (May, August and November). A total of fifty four (54) water
samples were collected using clean bottles and stored for laboratory analysis of water quality
level. The data obtained were subjected to analysis of variance (ANOVA) using Statistical
Application for Sciences (SAS, 2020). The results revealed that the water analysis the results
revealed that the concentration of primary cations were in order of Na+ >Ca2+ > K+ > Mg2+ while
for the anions increases in order of HCO3
- >SO4
2- >Cl- > CO3
2- > NO3. The IWQI ratings indicate
that suitability index for surface water irrigation practices were SAR, RSC, % Na, MH and PI,
while the unsuitable index were KI, PS and RSBC respectively. Moreover, the suitable indices for
ground water were found to be SAR, RSC, %Na, KI, PS and RSBC. Meanwhile the suitable indices
are MH and PI respectively. Therefore, surface water source in the area is suitable for irrigation
practices while the ground water is considered unsuitable and required treatment before usage.</jats:p>
title: An Empirical Evaluation of Surface and Ground Water Quality of River Chochi for Sustainable Food Production

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>We investigate the sensitivity of current and future hadron-collider experiments to axion-like particles (ALPs) through associated diboson production, focusing on a linear effective field theory framework with bosonic ALP couplings. We analyze the dominant production mechanisms and relevant backgrounds, considering the impact of jet misidentification rates on the diboson background. We present our results using conservative jet-misidentification rates, and derive four-dimensional constraints on the ALP couplings to gluons, weak bosons, and photons. Our findings highlight the potential of the high-luminosity phase of the CERN Large Hadron Collider to probe the ALP parameter space in the sub-GeV mass range, as well as the codependencies of the various ALP couplings.</jats:p>
title: Constraints on axion-like particles via associated diboson production in hadronic collisions

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Offshore wind is moving to larger turbines, deeper water and floating foundations while developers remain under pressure to reduce the levelised cost of energy (LCOE). This article presents a transparent, reproducible scenario model that links turbine reliability, availability, energy yield and LCOE, and it quantifies how much of a projected cost reduction comes from reliability and turbine scale and how much comes from exogenous cost and financing assumptions. Subsystem failure rates representative of a 97-turbine onshore fleet of 1.5 MW turbines are translated offshore with published stress factors and extrapolated to 8 MW and 15 MW ratings with explicit scaling laws. A Monte Carlo failure-and-repair simulation (10,000 turbine-years, fixed seed) returns availability, which enters the net capacity factor and hence the LCOE. Four scenarios are analysed: the onshore reference (S1), its offshore translation (S2), a 640 MW fixed-bottom farm (S3) and a 900 MW floating farm (S4). Central LCOE values are 119, 79.5 and 65.8 €/MWh for S2–S4, with input-uncertainty 90% intervals of 102–141, 68–95 and 56–88 €/MWh. A Shapley decomposition attributes the 53 €/MWh reduction from S2 to S4 to gross capacity factor (− 17.8), O&M cost per MW (− 15.4), CapEx per MW (− 14.1) and financing terms (− 13.8), partly offset by lower availability (+ 7.4). WACC, capacity factor and CapEx are the three most influential inputs in every offshore scenario, with failure rate fourth. The ranking S4 < S3 holds for mechanical scaling exponents up to about 0.8 but only if floating CapEx stays below 2.7 M€/MW; S3 and S4 are therefore conditional projections, not forecasts.</jats:p>
title: Comprehensive predictive models for offshore wind farm performance: integrating reliability, energy production and cost analysis for current and next-generation installations

items.abstract: <jats:p>A…B-type separable words, characterized by complex separated forms, semantic integration, and strong colloquiality, constitute a major difficulty in international Chinese language education. Focusing on the three major insertion types of separable words—particle insertion, attributive insertion, and complement insertion—this study follows the empirical procedures of speech-production research within the framework of code-switching theory and conducts a three-factor mixed experiment, recording production error rates and temporal costs for quantitative analysis. The results show that under the switching condition the main effect was significant and the switching cost was evident; separation type exerted a considerable influence on production cost, with attributive insertion incurring the largest cost and complement insertion the smallest; and the HSK 5 group showed lower switching costs and error rates than the HSK 4 group, with significant effects. The article argues that the teaching of A…B-type separable words in international Chinese language education should differentiate word structure types and learner profiles, and that the teaching of attributive insertion into separable words should run through the intermediate and advanced stages throughout.</jats:p>
title: An Empirical Study on the Production Difficulty of A...B Type Separable Words from the Perspective of Code-Switching

items.abstract: <jats:p>Exclusive breastfeeding during the first six months provides essential immunological protection and balanced nutrition for neonatal survival and maternal recovery. However, breast milk production may be affected by physiological, behavioral, and psychological factors. This study aimed to analyze factors influencing breast milk production among postpartum mothers at PMB Lusi Anggilia, Simpang Hulu, Ketapang Regency, West Kalimantan. An analytical observational study with a cross-sectional design involved 50 postpartum mothers (days 3–42), selected through total sampling. Data were collected using structured questionnaires assessing maternal knowledge, anxiety, husband's support, breastfeeding frequency, and breast milk smoothness. Spearman's Rank correlation was used for bivariate analysis (α = 0.05). Univariate results showed that 72.0% of respondents had good knowledge, 84.0% received high husband support, 74.0% breastfed fewer than eight times per day, and 60.0% experienced smooth milk production. Bivariate analysis revealed no significant relationship between maternal knowledge and breast milk production (r = 0.138, p = 0.338) or between breastfeeding frequency and breast milk production (r = 0.112, p = 0.440). Conversely, maternal anxiety had a strong, significant negative correlation with breast milk smoothness (r = -0.720, p < 0.001), making it the most dominant determinant. Husband's support also showed a significant positive relationship (r = 0.312, p = 0.028). These findings indicate that maternal psychological well-being and husband's involvement play crucial roles in facilitating the oxytocin-mediated milk ejection reflex. Therefore, midwifery interventions should prioritize postpartum mental health screening, stress-reduction counseling, and spousal empowerment to support successful lactation.</jats:p>
title: Factors Influencing Breast Milk Production among Postpartum Mothers at Independent Midwife Practice (PMB) Lusi Anggilia

items.abstract: <jats:p>Anaerobic digestion (AD) supports sustainable organic waste management, renewable energy generation and resource circularity. However, optimisation strategies prioritising methane yield may overlook energy requirements, fugitive emissions and resource recovery, potentially compromising overall environmental performance. This study critically examines the sustainability implications of AD optimisation research and identifies opportunities to integrate environmental, economic, and circular economy considerations into biogas production. A bibliometric and thematic review of 413 Scopus-indexed publications (2020–2025) was conducted using VOSviewer and Bibliometrix, complemented by a critical synthesis of optimisation approaches and sustainability-related findings. Research output increased from 40 publications in 2020 to 120 in 2025, representing a threefold increase, with a reported annual publication growth rate of 24.57%. Keyword co-occurrence analysis identified 45 frequently occurring keywords, organised into five interconnected research clusters: feedstock management, co-digestion, process optimisation and pretreatment, modelling and intelligent control, and sustainability and circular economy integration. The critical synthesis identifies energy–climate synergies and trade-offs, including reductions in processing energy and modelled emissions, as well as competing electricity-generation and climate outcomes across optimisation configurations. Although hybrid optimisation frameworks are increasingly discussed, consistent integration of life-cycle assessment, techno-economic evaluation, methane-loss mitigation and full-scale environmental validation remains an important research priority. This review proposes a conceptual multi-objective optimisation framework that integrates methane recovery, net energy performance, greenhouse gas emissions, economic viability, operational stability, and nutrient recovery; however, it requires further independent validation. These findings provide sustainability-oriented priorities for researchers, engineers and policymakers seeking to develop resource-efficient, environmentally responsible and economically viable biogas systems.</jats:p>
title: Sustainable Biogas Production Through Anaerobic Digestion: Environmental Trade-Offs, Process Optimisation and Circular Economy Pathways

<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Manufacturers have begun to experiment with gig labor due to persistent workforce shortages. This article develops impact pathways that specify what manufacturers must resolve for gig labor to function as an effective flexibility lever, and where operations and supply chain management (OSCM) research can advance implementation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We conducted 13 semi-structured interviews, 11 with manufacturing executives and two with CEOs of manufacturing-focused gig labor platforms. Transcripts were analyzed with a Gioia-style coding process.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We identify four impact pathways shaping whether gig labor can work in manufacturing: (1) designing flexible workflows for gig labor integration; (2) building plant-level legitimacy for hybrid core–gig workforces; (3) enablement of gig labor through platform mediation; and (4) governing the manufacturing gig labor supply chain. The pathways highlight implications for managers, platform designers, and policymakers. Managers should modularize suitable tasks, design quality into processes, and make the benefits of gig labor visible to incumbent workers. Platforms should embed skills-based matching without increasing income instability, and policymakers should assess whether safety, liability, and worker-classification rules fit flexible arrangements.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Gig labor research, developed mainly in consumer-facing platform settings, rests on a largely unexamined plug-and-play assumption in which tasks arrive pre-bounded, gig workers operate apart from a permanent workforce, workers are interchangeable, and governance is a two-party relationship between platform and worker. This article shows where each premise breaks down in a manufacturing context and offers a future research agenda for OSCM.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Impact pathways: flexibility on the factory floor – expanding gig labor research into the manufacturing context

items.abstract: <jats:p>„Семейният“ портрет разкрива основните ограничения, свързани с розопроизводството, пред които се изправя едно конкретно домакинство – несигурният пазар, климатичните промени и недостатъчната институционална подкрепа. В същото време решения се търсят в социалната солидарност, изпитаните практики и традиционното познание. Настоящата статия има за цел да представи едно от домакинствата на дребни розопроизводители в село Горно Черковище, намиращо се на 12 километра северно от град Казанлък. Благоприятният климат, географското разположение и наличието на значителни водни ресурси го правят подходящо място за отглеждане на т.нар. Rosa damascena Mill. (казанлъшка роза), произлизаща от добре познатата Rosa damascena. Според местното население, тя „вирее най-добре“ именно в тази част на Розовата долина и има „най-тежък цвят“. В селото розопроизводството се възприема като наследствен поминък, а семействата, вплели тази дейност в домашната си икономика, са около седем на брой. Следвайки метода „семейни портрети“ на Катрин Кокрейн, ще опиша и анализирам организацията и разпределението на труда във вътрешносемейната динамика, междупоколенческия опит и знание, както и различни стратегии на домакинството за устойчивост и препитание чрез този традиционен поминък.</jats:p>
title: Розопроизводството като препитание в едно подбалканско домакинство: антропологичен прочит по метода „семейни портрети“

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    In magnetically confined plasmas, energetic-particle (EP)-driven instabilities can induce redistribution and losses of energetic ions, thereby affecting plasma heating and confinement. In this work, fast-ion-driven beta-induced Alfvén eigenmode (BAE) excited by ion cyclotron resonance heating (ICRH) was investigated in low-density EAST plasmas using experimentally reconstructed equilibria and profiles. Experimentally, strong ICRH led to a significant increase in ion temperature and plasma stored energy, accompanied by the excitation of an Alfvén eigenmode at
                    <jats:inline-formula>
                      <jats:tex-math>
                        
                      </jats:tex-math>
                      <mml:math xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll">
                        <mml:mrow>
                          <mml:mo>∼</mml:mo>
                        </mml:mrow>
                      </mml:math>
                    </jats:inline-formula>
                    64
                    <jats:inline-formula>
                      <jats:tex-math>
                        
                      </jats:tex-math>
                      <mml:math xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll">
                        <mml:mrow>
                          <mml:mtext> </mml:mtext>
                          <mml:mrow>
                            <mml:mi>kHz</mml:mi>
                          </mml:mrow>
                        </mml:mrow>
                      </mml:math>
                    </jats:inline-formula>
                    under 1.6 MW heating power, while no such mode was observed at reduced power. Continuum analysis identified this mode as a core-localized BAE. To interpret these observations, integrated simulations combining TORIC, ASCOT, and GTC were performed. A modified fast-ion distribution function was implemented to capture the strong velocity-space anisotropy of ICRH-generated fast ions. Linear gyrokinetic simulations reproduced the observed BAE frequency and identified a threshold in fast-ion pressure for mode excitation. Orbit-following simulations with realistic wall geometry demonstrated that the BAE induces significant phase-space redistribution and enhances the loss of high-energy fast ions (energy
                    <jats:inline-formula>
                      <jats:tex-math>
                        
                      </jats:tex-math>
                      <mml:math xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll">
                        <mml:mrow>
                          <mml:mo>></mml:mo>
                          <mml:mn>600</mml:mn>
                          <mml:mtext> </mml:mtext>
                          <mml:mrow>
                            <mml:mi>keV</mml:mi>
                          </mml:mrow>
                        </mml:mrow>
                      </mml:math>
                    </jats:inline-formula>
                    ). Separately, the ASCOT power-deposition analysis shows that the strong BAE reduces the collisional power transferred from fast ions to thermal ions, thereby suppressing the fast-ion contribution to ion heating and limiting the increase in ion temperature. As the measured BAE activity decreases in Phase B, recovery of this ion-heating channel explains the subsequent rise in ion temperature. These results clarify the interplay between ICRH-generated fast ions, BAE activity, and ion heating, and provide insights into optimizing fast-ion confinement and heating efficiency in future burning plasma devices.
                  </jats:p>
title: Impact of ICRH-driven beta-induced Alfvén eigenmode on fast-ion redistribution and ion heating in EAST plasmas

<jats:p>
                    Water ice only appears on interstellar dust grains beyond a certain depth into a molecular cloud. This depth has so far been quoted as one extinction threshold per cloud. We measured the threshold along 43 009 sightlines through the Ophiuchus cloud with the ice color-excess method, which converts archival WISE and
                    <jats:italic>Spitzer</jats:italic>
                    photometry of background stars into the peak optical depth of the 3 μm water-ice band. We sorted the sightlines by the 12 μm surface brightness of the cloud at fixed extinction, a proxy for the ultraviolet field that excites the polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons at the cloud surface. The onset of ice formation lies at higher extinction toward sightlines with brighter 12 μm emission, ranging from
                    <jats:italic>A</jats:italic>
                    <jats:sub>
                      <jats:italic>K</jats:italic>
                      <jats:sub>
                        <jats:italic>S</jats:italic>
                      </jats:sub>
                    </jats:sub>
                    <jats:sup>th</jats:sup>
                     = 0.67 to 1.15 mag. It increases by 0.58 to 0.90 mag in
                    <jats:italic>A</jats:italic>
                    <jats:sub>
                      <jats:italic>K</jats:italic>
                      <jats:sub>
                        <jats:italic>S</jats:italic>
                      </jats:sub>
                    </jats:sub>
                    per factor of ten in 12 μm brightness, depending on the adopted reddening coefficient. Because the 12 μm-bright and -faint sightlines lie in different parts of the cloud, we repeated the comparison within each of the five subregions, and four of the subregions show the same trend. The trend also persists among sightlines with a similar amount of diffuse material around them. A later onset in more strongly irradiated gas is expected from photodesorption by external ultraviolet light, although a comparison of its size with models requires a calibration of the 12 μm brightness against the strength of the field. The extinction at which water ice appears thus varies with the local environment, which complicates comparisons between clouds. Photometric ice maps resolve this variation across entire clouds, and the SPHEREx and JWST ice surveys can test it spectroscopically.
                  </jats:p>
title: Water-ice formation in Ophiuchus follows the local irradiation

<jats:p>
                    Plasma-based accelerators are beginning to employ relativistic beams with unprecedented charge and ultrashort durations. These dense driver beams can drive wakes even in high-density plasmas (
                    <a:math xmlns:a="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline">
                      <a:mrow>
                        <a:mo>≳</a:mo>
                        <a:msup>
                          <a:mrow>
                            <a:mn>10</a:mn>
                          </a:mrow>
                          <a:mrow>
                            <a:mn>19</a:mn>
                          </a:mrow>
                        </a:msup>
                        <a:mtext> </a:mtext>
                        <a:mtext> </a:mtext>
                        <a:mrow>
                          <a:msup>
                            <a:mrow>
                              <a:mi>cm</a:mi>
                            </a:mrow>
                            <a:mrow>
                              <a:mo>−</a:mo>
                              <a:mn>3</a:mn>
                            </a:mrow>
                          </a:msup>
                        </a:mrow>
                      </a:mrow>
                    </a:math>
                    ), where betatron radiation becomes increasingly important and begins to affect the dynamics of the accelerated beam. We show that betatron cooling leads to a strong structuring of the phase space of the beam. This gives rise to bunched, ring-like structures with positive radial position and momentum gradients, i.e., population inversion of the amplitude of oscillation. We derive the characteristic timescales for this process analytically and confirm our predictions with multidimensional particle-in-cell simulations. The radiation-dominated regime of beam dynamics fundamentally alters the acceleration process and produces self-structured beams; particle-in-cell simulations of the resulting beams show that it becomes unstable to the ion-channel laser and lead to exponential amplification of radiation.
                  </jats:p>
title: Phase-Space Shaping Due to Betatron Cooling in Wakefield Accelerators and the Onset of the Ion-Channel Laser

items.abstract: <jats:p>Real-time process monitoring during high-speed laser drilling remains a critical challenge in modern manufacturing, where industrial laser systems operate at repetition rates of up to several hundred kilohertz [D. Franz et al., Materials 15, 3932 (2022)], with next-generation systems targeting the megahertz regime [S. Janssen et al., Proc. SPIE 13350, 1335007 (2025)]. As each ablating laser pulse creates a tiny plasma with material-specific emission lines, laser-induced breakdown spectroscopy could be used to enable process monitoring. However, existing laser-induced breakdown spectroscopy (LIBS) approaches so far are limited to kilohertz acquisition rates [R. Noll, Laser-Induced Breakdown Spectroscopy: Fundamentals and Applications (Springer, Berlin, 2012)], three orders of magnitude too slow for inline monitoring and closed-loop control at industrial processing speeds. We present a high-speed LIBS sensor capable of per-pulse material analysis at repetition rates exceeding 1 MHz, enabling real-time feedback during laser microvia drilling in printed circuit boards (PCBs). The system detects the copper atomic emission line at 521.8 nm using a narrow bandpass filter combined with high-speed photodetection and custom analog signal processing, achieving complete signal acquisition within the 1 μs interpulse period at 1 MHz. Time-resolved plasma emission characterization reveals the nanosecond-scale temporal dynamics and validates the temporal gating approach for background suppression. Comprehensive validation against conventional spectrometer-based LIBS across multilayer PCB structures demonstrates equivalent material classification performance, confirmed by laser scanning microscopy. Microvia drilling experiments with position-resolved material detection demonstrate accurate real-time material classification throughout the drilling process. A retrospective analysis of the acquired position-resolved data indicates that applying a closed-loop termination strategy could reduce laser pulse count by 18.6% on average and up to 25.6% in favorable cases, compared to conventional fixed-pulse protocols. These results establish MHz-rate LIBS as a viable approach for inline quality control and adaptive process feedback at time scales relevant to industrial laser micromachining.</jats:p>
title: Pulse-resolved laser-induced breakdown spectroscopy for inline monitoring of microvia drilling in printed circuit boards at MHz repetition rates

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Large-scale inspection requires both dense surface data and a stable global reference, which are difficult to obtain with a single instrument. This paper proposes a joint measurement method integrating a laser scanner, a stereo-vision tracking unit, and a laser tracker. In the proposed method, the scanner captures dense local surface data, the stereo-vision unit determines the scanner pose, and the laser tracker establishes the global reference by observing a scanner-mounted spherically mounted retroreflector (SMR). Paired observations of the same SMR center connect the tracking and laser-tracker frames, forming a unified coordinate chain that transforms local point clouds into the global frame. To ensure the accuracy of this joint measurement chain, a depth-stratified calibration-position design is further introduced to account for distance-dependent stereo uncertainty. The 3–6 m working volume is divided into near, middle, and far ranges, and eleven 12-position layouts are assessed by Monte Carlo simulation and repeated experiments. The results show that middle-dominated mixed-depth layouts consistently achieve low error levels, with the 3/6/3 (S7) and 2/8/2 (S8) near/middle/far configurations showing particularly favorable performance. For S7, the mean SMR-center consistency residuals are 0.101 mm and 0.106 mm for the fixed and estimated SMR-center modes, respectively, corresponding to reductions of 13.1% and 11.5% relative to the near-only layout. These results support distance-aware calibration-position planning for the 3–6 m, 12-position configuration investigated in this study and the proposed cross-system coordinate framework.</jats:p>
title: A joint measurement method integrating stereo-vision-tracked laser scanning and laser-tracker referencing: depth-stratified calibration-position design

items.abstract: <jats:p>Machine learning now reaches every stage of transcription factor (TF) drug discovery, but its contribution falls sharply along the evidence hierarchy. This review works through five tiers of evidence, from sequence and transcriptome through protein structure, cellular phenotype and chemical matter to clinical validation, and examines recent progress and the strength of evidence at each. Unified models can now predict binding, accessibility and expression within a single framework, and the definition of a ligandable site has widened from a static cavity to a transient conformational state, so disordered regions are no longer excluded a priori. The downstream tiers are far thinner. Molecular generation keeps improving geometric plausibility, but a unified benchmark shows that such metrics do not track the ability to produce active molecules, and no clinical intervention to date can be traced to substantive machine learning input. Missing trivial baselines and information leakage also make retrospective evaluation systematically optimistic. What limits machine learning at each tier appears to be the supply of verifiable labels more than model capacity. TFs sit upstream of regulation, so a single successful intervention may correct an entire downstream expression programme, which keeps them attractive for diseases that still lack usable targets and demanding as a test of algorithmic prediction. On this reading, further gains for TFs and other undruggable targets depend more on what each tier can be made to measure than on new architectures.</jats:p>
title: Machine Learning for Transcription Factor Target Discovery and Drug Intervention: Progress, Challenges and Outlook
