items.abstract:
<jats:p>Radiation has always been present and is all around us. Life has evolved in a world containing
significant levels of ionizing radiation. Our bodies are adopted to it. Background exposure from
normal levels of the naturally occurring radioactive materials (NORMS) are present in all
environmental materials and do not vary remarkably from place to place. Where human activities
(Laboratory activities, pollution mining and others) have increased the relative concentration of
the radionuclides, they are referred to as the technologically enhanced naturally occurring
radioactive materials. Certain types of building materials are known to be radioactive. Exposure
to indoor ionizing radiation like exposure to any other type of ionizing radiation results in critical
health challenges. The aim of this research work is to determine the level of indoor and outdoor
ionizing radiation in some science laboratories in federal college of education, Yola, These science
laboratories usually harbour a number of active radiation sources. The ionizing radiation levels
were measured using gamma scout (model GS2 with serial number, for the data collection 20
readings were taking for indoor and outdoor and the data measured were read on the display
screen of the gamma-scout device. The gamma-scout hand held device was used obtained data for
the study was adjusted to detect the alpha, beta and gamma types of radiation in µSv/hr. The mean
equivalent dose rate per hour for indoor background ionizing radiation for the laboratories was
found to be 0.012mSv/hr while the outdoor was 0.084µSv/hr. The mean annual equivalent dose
rate of the laboratories ware compute for indoor and outdoor background radiation level to be
0.013mSv/yr and 0.22mSv/yr respectively, and it concluded that all the science laboratories in the
study are in a good proportion below the world wide average dose of 2.4mSv/yr.it was
recommended that periodic measurement of ionizing radiation level checking should be done all
doors and windows of laboratories are open daily in other to expel some accumulated redox gases.</jats:p>
title: Evaluation of Background Ionizing Radiation Level in Some Science Laboratories in Federal College of Education Yola

                            <mml:mn>3</mml:mn>
                          </mml:msub>
                        </mml:mrow>
                      </mml:math>
                    </jats:inline-formula>
                    ) are assessed for operational lifetime strategies. Initial optimisation identifies breeder-to-multiplier volumetric ratios that maximise TBR at time zero, followed by time-dependent simulations to quantify TBR degradation due to lithium depletion during service. It is shown that while higher initial multiplier fractions enhance TBR, they also accelerate lithium depletion, reducing blanket lifetime. Conversely, hybrid ceramics with intrinsic neutron multiplication show reduced sensitivity to additional multipliers. A novel layer-wise optimisation approach, varying breeder and multiplier distributions radially and poloidally, is shown to extend blanket lifetimes and maintain TBR above the critical threshold for longer periods demonstrating lifetime limitations may be elsewhere within the breeder blanket. Verification against FISPACT-II confirms the accuracy of the OpenMC depletion methodology utilised. The results highlight the importance of spatially optimised material distributions and lithium inventory management in maximising breeder blanket longevity. This work provides a robust framework for the design of next-generation solid breeder blankets, offering practical strategies to minimise replacement frequency and support sustainable fusion energy.
                  </jats:p>
title: Tritium breeding lifetime assessment of a ceramic-based blanket in a fusion tokamak device

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    Radiopharmaceutical information in imaging systems is typically recorded as free text or as flat code system entries that include little or no computable information about radionuclides’ physical properties. This article introduces the Nuclide and Element Ontology (NUCLEON), a machine-processable knowledge resource that represents the 118 known chemical elements and 5408 nuclides, including 2019 metastable isomers, with computable nuclear properties. The ontology declares each element and nuclide as both a class and an individual: the class structure generates a taxonomy that aligns with vocabularies of chemistry and clinical medicine, and the individual entities support quantitative assertions, such as half-life. Each of 7691 decay branches is an individual specifying its mode of decay and branching ratio; 7399 branches have an explicit link to their decay product (daughter) nuclide, derived from the decay mode rather than transcribed. Ground-state data were taken from the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) LiveChart of Nuclides, isomer data from the NUBASE2020 evaluation, and the energies and yields of 3990 radiation emissions of clinically coded radionuclides and their decay chains from International Commission on Radiological Protection (ICRP) Publication 107; symbols and names were verified against standard chemical nomenclature. NUCLEON is linked to the Ontology of Chemical Elements, SNOMED Clinical Terms, and DICOM radiopharmaceutical isotope and PET radionuclide code sequences, allowing a nuclide to be resolved directly from a DICOM header. The ontology incorporates 215,862 triples across 5533 classes and 17,253 named individuals. Automated checks confirmed the arithmetic consistency of atomic, neutron, and mass numbers, and none of the derived decay products disagreed with ICRP Publication 107 or the Evaluated Nuclear Structure Data File. Element names are provided in seven languages. NUCLEON is available at
                    <jats:ext-link xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" xlink:href="https://bioportal.bioontology.org/ontologies/NUCLEON" ext-link-type="uri">https://bioportal.bioontology.org/ontologies/NUCLEON</jats:ext-link>
                    .
                  </jats:p>

The saturation level and the resulting EP transport are examined. This provides data for future inter-code nonlinear benchmarking. In
                    <jats:monospace>TEK</jats:monospace>
                    , all species (electrons, thermal ions, EPs) are treated on the same footing using the gyrokinetic model (with electrons in the zero Larmor radius limit). The electromagnetic cancellation problem is mitigated by using the mixed-variable pullback method. Numerical details related to electromagnetic gyrokinetic simulation are discussed.
                  </jats:p>
title: Linear and nonlinear benchmark of gyrokinetic simulation of energetic particle driven toroidal Alfvén eigenmodes in ITPA TAE benchmark case

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    In magnetically confined plasmas, energetic-particle (EP)-driven instabilities can induce redistribution and losses of energetic ions, thereby affecting plasma heating and confinement. In this work, fast-ion-driven beta-induced Alfvén eigenmode (BAE) excited by ion cyclotron resonance heating (ICRH) was investigated in low-density EAST plasmas using experimentally reconstructed equilibria and profiles. Experimentally, strong ICRH led to a significant increase in ion temperature and plasma stored energy, accompanied by the excitation of an Alfvén eigenmode at
                    <jats:inline-formula>
                      <jats:tex-math>
                        
                      </jats:tex-math>
                      <mml:math xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll">
                        <mml:mrow>
                          <mml:mo>∼</mml:mo>
                        </mml:mrow>
                      </mml:math>
                    </jats:inline-formula>
                    64
                    <jats:inline-formula>
                      <jats:tex-math>
                        
                      </jats:tex-math>
                      <mml:math xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll">
                        <mml:mrow>
                          <mml:mtext> </mml:mtext>
                          <mml:mrow>
                            <mml:mi>kHz</mml:mi>
                          </mml:mrow>
                        </mml:mrow>
                      </mml:math>
                    </jats:inline-formula>
                    under 1.6 MW heating power, while no such mode was observed at reduced power. Continuum analysis identified this mode as a core-localized BAE. To interpret these observations, integrated simulations combining TORIC, ASCOT, and GTC were performed. A modified fast-ion distribution function was implemented to capture the strong velocity-space anisotropy of ICRH-generated fast ions. Linear gyrokinetic simulations reproduced the observed BAE frequency and identified a threshold in fast-ion pressure for mode excitation. Orbit-following simulations with realistic wall geometry demonstrated that the BAE induces significant phase-space redistribution and enhances the loss of high-energy fast ions (energy
                    <jats:inline-formula>
                      <jats:tex-math>
                        
                      </jats:tex-math>
                      <mml:math xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll">
                        <mml:mrow>
                          <mml:mo>></mml:mo>
                          <mml:mn>600</mml:mn>
                          <mml:mtext> </mml:mtext>
                          <mml:mrow>
                            <mml:mi>keV</mml:mi>
                          </mml:mrow>
                        </mml:mrow>
                      </mml:math>
                    </jats:inline-formula>
                    ). Separately, the ASCOT power-deposition analysis shows that the strong BAE reduces the collisional power transferred from fast ions to thermal ions, thereby suppressing the fast-ion contribution to ion heating and limiting the increase in ion temperature. As the measured BAE activity decreases in Phase B, recovery of this ion-heating channel explains the subsequent rise in ion temperature. These results clarify the interplay between ICRH-generated fast ions, BAE activity, and ion heating, and provide insights into optimizing fast-ion confinement and heating efficiency in future burning plasma devices.
                  </jats:p>
title: Impact of ICRH-driven beta-induced Alfvén eigenmode on fast-ion redistribution and ion heating in EAST plasmas

items.abstract: <jats:p>The evolving nature of terrorism in West Africa has underscored the importance of intelligence-led counterterrorism strategies capable of addressing increasingly sophisticated and transnational threats. Violent extremist organisations, such as Jama'at Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin (JNIM), the Islamic State West Africa Province (ISWAP), Boko Haram, and other affiliated armed groups, continue to exploit porous borders, weak institutional coordination, limited intelligence interoperability, and governance deficits to expand their operational reach across the region. Although West African states have established various national and regional mechanisms to facilitate intelligence collection, analysis, and dissemination, persistent challenges associated with institutional fragmentation, political mistrust, legal constraints, technological disparities, and resource limitations continue to undermine effective intelligence sharing. This paper examines the strategic role of national and regional fusion centres in enhancing counterterrorism intelligence cooperation across West Africa. Drawing on secondary data, the paper evaluates existing intelligence-sharing frameworks, identifies operational challenges, and proposes practical strategies for strengthening intelligence fusion mechanisms. The study argues that effective intelligence fusion centres can enhance situational awareness, improve coordination, strengthen early-warning systems, and facilitate collective responses, thereby increasing regional resilience against terrorism and promoting lasting peace and security in West Africa.</jats:p>
title: Enhancing counterterrorism intelligence and information sharing: Strengthening regional and national fusion Centers in West Africa

items.abstract: <jats:p>Diabetic retinopathy (DR) is the leading cause of preventable blindness in adults and poses an increasing challenge with the global rise in diabetes. Traditional screening, based on human image analysis, is limited by high costs, subjectivity, and a shortage of trained specialists. In this context, artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a promising alternative, enabling automated screening with high accuracy and efficiency. This review, conducted in accordance with PRISMA 2020 guidelines, evaluated studies published between 2015 and 2025 on the use of AI for the early diagnosis of DR. Fourteen studies involving more than 50,000 patients across diverse clinical and socioeconomic settings were included. Deep learning models — particularly convolutional neural networks (CNNs) — achieved sensitivities ranging from 86% to 99% and specificities between 89% and 99%, with areas under the curve typically exceeding 0.95. Systems such as ARDA and EyeArt demonstrated diagnostic performance comparable to that of human experts and feasibility for implementation in population-based primary care screening programs.</jats:p>
title: Artificial intelligence in the diagnosis of diabetic retinopathy: a systematic review of diagnostic accuracy and clinical impact (2015–2025)

items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec id="j_dx-2026-0166_abs_001">
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>To trace how a suspected but unexamined surgical complication propagated through non-disclosure, anchoring, and fragmented care into months of diagnostic delay, unresolved illness, and lasting harm.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec id="j_dx-2026-0166_abs_002">
                    <jats:title>Case presentation</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A 23-year-old woman developed persistent clear nasal drainage after elective functional endoscopic sinus surgery and asked her surgeon whether it was a cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) leak. Beta-2 transferrin was never ordered. The complication was never confirmed or excluded. In March of her first year of medical school, at 24, she became acutely ill. An early lumbar puncture was reported to her as viral meningitis and not investigated further. That record is lost, and the only surviving lumbar puncture was essentially normal. Over many months she cycled through various emergency departments, dismissed as drug-seeking and a frequent flier, then was committed to a psychiatric unit. She had seizures before receiving intravenous treatment for presumed Lyme meningitis and for toxoplasmosis supported by elevated Toxoplasma IgM and IgG. Medical school ended. Cognitive impairment and fatigue persist 20 years later.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec id="j_dx-2026-0166_abs_003">
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The failure was not one missed clue but a cascade in which each error made the next more likely: a suspected leak became an incomplete history, then a confident but incorrect psychiatric closure. Two mechanisms stand out: a private workup withheld from the treating team, and an illness that corrupted the patient’s symptom reporting and generated false histories clinicians anchored upon, even as her core account, that her illness was organic, stayed correct. Disclosure, ownership of the whole picture, and repeated reassessment can interrupt such a cascade.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Conservative management: diagnostic error after suspected CSF leak

                  <jats:p>
                    We study the effect of temperature on composition-driven
                    <jats:italic>g</jats:italic>
                    -modes in the cores of warm neutron stars. Using a chiral
                    <jats:italic>SU</jats:italic>
                    (2)
                    <jats:sub>
                      <jats:italic>f</jats:italic>
                    </jats:sub>
                    sigma model, we construct isentropic equations of state and stellar configurations for hot and dense matter. Weak-interaction rates are incorporated into a complex, frequency-dependent dynamical sound speed that approaches the frozen-composition limit for slow reactions and the beta-equilibrated limit for fast reactions. We solve self-consistently for the complex
                    <jats:italic>g</jats:italic>
                    -mode eigenfrequency and find that its real part depends nonmonotonically on the nuclear symmetry-energy slope parameter
                    <jats:italic>L</jats:italic>
                    , reaching its largest values near
                    <jats:italic>L</jats:italic>
                     ≈ 100–110 MeV. Increasing the entropy per baryon accelerates chemical reequilibration and suppresses the oscillation frequency. The associated damping rate reaches a maximum when the weak-interaction relaxation and mode timescales become comparable, signifying that dissipative effects also depend on
                    <jats:italic>L</jats:italic>
                    . Our results demonstrate that the thermal weak-interaction response and the density dependence of the symmetry energy jointly determine the
                    <jats:italic>g</jats:italic>
                    -mode spectrum of warm neutron stars.
                  </jats:p>

items.abstract: <jats:p>Prenatal genetic testing has undergone a remarkable transformation over the past two decades. Powered by genomic medicine, carrier screening, cell-free DNA screening, chromosomal microarray, exome sequencing, and genome sequencing have augmented the ability of obstetric care clinicians to diagnose fetal chromosomal imbalances and single-gene disorders and counsel patients on the clinical implications. Carrier screening with gene panels can identify asymptomatic carriers of a multitude of conditions, whereas cell-free DNA screening allows greater detection of aneuploidy with lower false-positive rates than ever thought possible. Prenatal diagnostic testing no longer involves simply looking at the structure of chromosomes. Chromosomal microarray analysis is capable of precisely identifying small areas of genomic imbalance, providing insight into affected genes. Next-generation sequencing–based diagnostic tests—targeted gene panels, exome sequencing, and genome sequencing—enable the diagnosis of many monogenic disorders prenatally and can provide a diagnosis in up to 25% of additional pregnancies with structural fetal anomalies compared with chromosomal microarray alone. An understanding of these tests will help obstetric care clinicians discuss available screening and diagnostic prenatal genetic tests with patients and explain their benefits, caveats, limitations, and results.</jats:p>
title: Prenatal Screening and Diagnostic Testing in the Era of Genomic Medicine

<jats:p>
                    <jats:italic>Context.</jats:italic>
                    For the typical modelling of neutron-star cooling after an accretion episode in low-mass X-ray binaries, an extra heating source of unknown physical origin, i.e. the shallow heating, is invoked in order to account for the inferred highly effective temperatures of the star up to hundreds of days after the end of accretion. The amount of shallow heating generated in the crust is usually taken to be proportional to the accretion rate, although the proportionality constant may change from source to source.
                  </jats:p>
                  <jats:p>
                    <jats:italic>Aims.</jats:italic>
                    We intend to model the effective temperature data of eight outburst episodes from seven different sources (MXB 1659-29, XTE J1701-462, EXO 0748-676, IGR J17480-2446 (Ter5 X-2), Swift J174805.3-244637 (Ter5 X-3), 1RXS J180408.9-342058, and KS 1731-260) without ad hoc shallow heating but accounting for the presence of thermonuclear heating due to the burning of the accreted
                    <jats:sup>1</jats:sup>
                    H and
                    <jats:sup>4</jats:sup>
                    He.
                  </jats:p>
                  <jats:p>
                    <jats:italic>Methods.</jats:italic>
                    We employed the fully relativistic code
                    <jats:monospace>NSCool</jats:monospace>
                    , which simulates both the crust and the core of a neutron star, equipped with a new boundary condition at the envelope–crust transition that considers thermonuclear heating leakage from the envelope into the crust and depends on the mass-accretion rate.
                  </jats:p>
                  <jats:p>
                    <jats:italic>Results.</jats:italic>
                    We find that the neutron star cooling for four out of eight of these outbursts can be well explained with this new boundary condition and without the requirement of extra shallow heating. For the remaining sources, an enhanced mass-accretion rate or high crustal impurities are needed to fit the observations.
                  </jats:p>
title: A re-examination of neutron star cooling in transient sources

items.abstract: <jats:p>Fluoride-salt-cooled high-temperature reactors and molten-salt reactors need compact, fouling-resistant primary-to-secondary heat exchangers that operate near atmospheric pressure at about 650 °C. Twisted tubes are a baffle-free, self-supporting candidate, but the available correlations cover narrow Reynolds number and modified Froude number windows and leave the shell side weakly characterized. Heat-transfer and friction correlations are developed for both sides of three stainless-steel twisted-tube heat exchangers, two of which differ only in twist pitch (101.6 and 76.2 mm) and one of which has a larger cross-section. Heat-transfer rates and pressure drops were measured in a counterflow water loop at 61 operating points, and the same geometries were modeled with steady Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes (RANS) simulations. Because the shell-side pressure drop, 4.6 to 25.7 Pa, fell below the transducer resolution and the measurements give only the overall thermal resistance, the Nusselt numbers and friction factors were reduced from the simulations, which the measurements were then used to test. The simulated values follow power laws in within 2.3% and 1.8% over tube-side from 14,000 to 50,000 and shell-side from 1560 to 3070. Shortening the pitch from 101.6 to 76.2 mm raises the shell-side and tube-side Nusselt numbers by 15% and 6% at equal , at the cost of 72% and 19% higher friction factors, and the tube-side Nusselt numbers of the long tubes exceed the smooth-tube value by 30 to 55%. The measured convective resistance agrees with the prediction in the median for Tube 1 and differs from it by 31% and 34% for Tubes 2 and 3, which is attributed to the energy imbalance between the streams. The measured tube-side friction factors are a constant 0.50 of the simulated values for the long tubes, a factor attributed to the shape of the inner cross-section of the formed tubes, which was not measured, so the friction correlations rest on the simulations. On a Reynolds-number basis the correlations lie within the band of published twisted-tube data. The correlations apply to the two cross-sections tested and within the stated ranges.</jats:p>
title: Numerical and Experimental Investigations of Heat Transfer and Pressure Drop for Twisted-Tube Heat Exchangers

items.abstract: <jats:p>Environment-perception modules underpin autonomous driving system operation for complex road scene comprehension. Three-dimensional (3D) object detection completes localization and classification work for road traffic participants including vehicles, pedestrians and cyclists. Camera sensors deliver rich texture and semantic data with performance degradation under low-light, fog and heavy-rain conditions. Millimeter-wave radar supports all-weather range and radial-velocity measurement with sparse point-cloud output and limited semantic discrimination capacity. Multi-modal fusion technology leverages complementary sensor characteristics for perception robustness improvement. This paper conducts millimeter-wave radar analysis covering historical evolution, working principle and core sensor characteristics. It compares sensor complementary attributes and three mainstream fusion paradigms, namely data-level, decision-level and feature-level fusion, to build the analysis basis for representative bird's-eye view (BEV) based Transformer cross-attention fusion networks. Technical bottlenecks covering space-time misalignment, modality imbalance and computing overhead are sorted out for subsequent discussion of practical engineering constraints and promising research directions in this field. Engineering-oriented suggestions are finally provided covering online calibration, model compression, physical-prior embedding and adverse-weather data augmentation.</jats:p>
title: Millimeter‑Wave Radar and Camera Multi‑modal Fusion for 3D Object Detection in Autonomous Driving

items.abstract: <jats:p>Background: Infertility is a major global reproductive health problem affecting individuals and couples across diverse populations. It is defined as failure to achieve pregnancy after 12 months or more of regular unprotected sexual intercourse and may result from female factors, male factors, combined abnormalities, or unexplained causes. Increasing maternal age, delayed childbearing, obesity, metabolic disorders, sexually transmitted infections, lifestyle-related factors, environmental exposures, and changing reproductive patterns have contributed to the growing complexity of infertility. Objective: This review aims to provide an updated overview of the major etiological factors responsible for male and female infertility, contemporary approaches to diagnostic evaluation, established and emerging risk factors, and recent advances in reproductive medicine. Methods: A narrative review of recent literature was undertaken focusing on publications addressing the epidemiology, etiology, diagnostic evaluation, reproductive infections, endocrine and metabolic disorders, lifestyle factors, environmental exposures, oxidative stress, reproductive tract microbiome, genetic factors, and emerging diagnostic technologies in infertility. Recent international recommendations and guidelines, including those from the World Health Organization and major reproductive medicine societies, were considered. Results: Infertility is a multifactorial disorder involving abnormalities of ovulation, ovarian reserve, tubal patency, uterine anatomy, endometriosis, spermatogenesis, sperm function, endocrine regulation, and genetic factors. Advancing reproductive age remains one of the strongest predictors of declining fertility. PCOS, obesity, diabetes, thyroid dysfunction, endometriosis, sexually transmitted infections, genital tuberculosis, smoking, alcohol consumption, psychological stress, and sedentary lifestyle may further impair reproductive potential. Increasing evidence suggests that environmental pollutants, endocrine-disrupting chemicals, oxidative stress, epigenetic mechanisms, and alterations of the vaginal and endometrial microbiome may contribute to infertility. Conventional investigations, including semen analysis, assessment of ovulation, ovarian reserve testing, ultrasonography, and evaluation of tubal patency, remain the foundation of diagnosis. Emerging approaches involving sperm DNA fragmentation testing, reproductive genetics, microbiome profiling, metabolomics, proteomics, and artificial intelligence-assisted assessment are expanding the diagnostic landscape, although several require further validation before routine clinical implementation. Conclusion: Infertility should be approached as a complex condition affecting both partners and requiring individualized, evidence-based evaluation. Early identification of modifiable risk factors, prevention of reproductive tract infections, healthy lifestyle practices, and timely assessment can improve reproductive outcomes. Future infertility care is likely to increasingly integrate conventional clinical evaluation with molecular diagnostics, reproductive microbiology, genetics, artificial intelligence, and personalized medicine. Ensuring affordable, equitable, and patient-centered access to infertility services should remain a major global reproductive health priority.</jats:p>
title: Infertility: An Updated Review of Etiology, Diagnostic Evaluation and Emerging Risk Factors

items.abstract: <jats:p>This study examines English–Arabic code-mixing in the naturally occurring interactions of Jordanian gamers during AI-supported online multiplayer gameplay sessions. Drawing on a structural–functional approach to bilingual gaming discourse, this study investigates the structural patterns and communicative functions of code-mixing and the reasons reported by participants for using English expressions within predominantly Arabic discourse. Data were collected from 30 authentic gameplay sessions involving 30 Jordanian Arabic–English bilingual gamers in the age range of 18–25 years. The gameplay sessions included gameplay recordings of widely played multiplayer games such as Fortnite, PUBG, Call of Duty, and Free Fire. The recorded interactions were transcribed and coded according to the structural type and interactional function, while an open-ended postsession questionnaire was used to explore the motivations for code-mixing among participants. The analysis identified three main functions: tactical efficiency, identity and role indexing, and the retention of game-specific terminology. All 20 illustrative excerpts were classified as intrasentential insertions, with English words and conventionalised gaming expressions embedded within predominantly Arabic grammatical frames. Participants used English to communicate tactical information concisely, retain official game terminology, evaluate player performance, and demonstrate familiarity with wider gaming culture. Furthermore, questionnaire responses suggested that code-mixing was associated with repeated exposure to English gaming content, communicative efficiency, participation in gaming communities, identity expression, and perceptions of English as the language of technology and contemporary gaming. AI-supported features, including matchmaking, bot-controlled actions, automated moderation, and anticheat systems, formed part of the broader sociotechnical environment in which the interaction occurred. However, the data did not show that AI directly caused the observed code-mixing. The findings demonstrate that English–Arabic code-mixing functions as a practical and socially meaningful bilingual resource that supports coordination, precision, identity construction, and participation in transnational gaming culture.</jats:p>
title: Linguistic fusion in AI-supported online gaming: English–Arabic code-mixing among gamers

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Diagnosis of group A streptococcus (GAS) pharyngitis depends on oropharyngeal swab specimens which are difficult to obtain outside clinical settings. Limited tolerance of children for oropharyngeal swab collection and the potential benefits of a home or over-the-counter (OTC) test for GAS pharyngitis have generated interest in other specimen types including saliva and mouth swabs, however, their performance has not been systematically reviewed. We conducted a systematic review of studies assessing the performance of alternate sample types in diagnosing GAS pharyngitis compared to oropharyngeal swabs.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We searched PubMed, Embase and Scopus systematically, retrieved 2462 records and imported them into the web-based platform Covidence. Duplicate entries numbering 1616 were removed leaving 846 records which underwent title and abstract screening to exclude 811. After full text assessment of thirty-five studies for eligibility, twelve were included for extraction and qualitative synthesis.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Of seventeen instances, from the twelve studies, in which saliva and other samples were compared against oropharyngeal swabs for the diagnosis of GAS pharyngitis using different assays, observed sensitivity and specificity ranged from 0–100% and 91–100%, respectively. Only five of the seventeen comparisons observed a sensitivity above 85%. Most of the studies had considerable risk of bias and concerns regarding applicability.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The performance of saliva and other samples in diagnosing GAS pharyngitis, compared against an oropharyngeal standard, has been investigated by some studies, however, most were insufficiently powered and had a substantial risk of bias. More adequately powered, appropriately designed studies are needed to draw valid inferences.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Diagnostic performance of oral sample types compared to oropharyngeal swab for detection of group A streptococcal pharyngitis: a systematic review

<jats:p>Rabies is a viral disease of major importance to public health and veterinary medicine due to its high case-fatality rate and potential for transmission between animals and humans. Caused by viruses of the genus Lyssavirus, the disease affects mammals and exhibits tropism for the central nervous system, resulting in progressive neurological manifestations and, in most cases, death. Among domestic animals, cats are susceptible hosts and may participate in the epidemiological cycle of the disease, particularly when exposed to infected animals.
In cats, the clinical presentation of rabies may vary and include behavioral changes, aggression, excessive vocalization, neurological abnormalities, difficulty swallowing, paralysis, and progression to death. Diagnosis is of fundamental importance because the clinical signs may resemble those of other neurological diseases, making laboratory confirmation necessary through specific diagnostic methods.
In addition to its clinical and diagnostic aspects, the occurrence of rabies in cats has significant epidemiological relevance due to its zoonotic nature. Animal vaccination, epidemiological surveillance, control of potentially infected animals, and implementation of preventive measures are essential to reduce disease transmission. Therefore, this review aims to address the main clinical, diagnostic, and epidemiological aspects of rabies in cats, emphasizing its importance in veterinary medicine and public health.</jats:p>
title: Raiva felina: revisão dos aspectos clínicos, diagnósticos e epidemiológicos
Feline rabies: a review of clinical, diagnostic, and epidemiological aspects

items.abstract:
<jats:p>Background: Multimodal artificial intelligence (AI) models are increasingly used for image-based diagnostic tasks, but their performance relative to oral and maxillofacial surgery trainees remains uncertain. This study compared the diagnostic performance of 3 contemporary multimodal AI models with oral and maxillofacial surgery residents and early-career specialists using New England Journal of Medicine (NEJM) Image Challenge cases.
Methods: In this single-center cross-sectional study, 49 human participants (44 residents and 5 specialists) completed a 50-item, image-based, 5-option diagnostic test derived from NEJM Image Challenge cases. The same cases were independently administered to generative pretrained transformer (GPT)-5.6 sol, Gemini 3.6 Flash, and Claude Sonnet 5 under standardized conditions without web access. The primary outcome was diagnostic accuracy. Human performance was also assessed by experience level, and item difficulty, test reliability, AI ranking, and error patterns were examined.
Results: Mean human accuracy was 50.8% (25.39 ± 7.02/50), with good internal consistency (Kuder–Richardson formula 20 = 0.816). Scores increased with experience (Spearman’s rho = 0.401, P = .004). Gemini achieved 88.0% accuracy, Claude 76.0%, and GPT-5.6 Sol 74.0%, each exceeding the mean of every human experience subgroup. Artificial intelligence performance remained comparatively high in items answered correctly by fewer than half of human participants. Four cases were missed by all 3 models, with identical incorrect alternatives selected in each.
Conclusion: Multimodal AI models outperformed the average human participant in this closedset image-based test, particularly in diagnostically difficult cases. However, shared systematic errors and benchmark-related limitations support their use as supervised educational and diagnostic support tools rather than autonomous diagnostic systems.</jats:p>
title: Diagnostic Performance of Multimodal Artificial Intelligence and Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery Clinicians: A Cross-Sectional Comparison Study

items.abstract: <jats:p>Laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) Ti–6Al–4V shows orientation-dependent fatigue behavior that tensile properties and bulk density do not fully explain. Vertical (VT) and horizontal (HZ) specimens were annealed at 850 °C for 2 h (furnace cooling) and characterized by optical and scanning electron microscopy, X-ray diffraction (XRD) with Rietveld refinement, micro-computed tomography (micro-CT), Vickers hardness, tensile tests, and high-cycle fatigue tests (R = 0.1). The annealed material consisted of α + β (approximately 88–92 vol.% α and 8–12 vol.% β). Tensile properties of the two orientations were similar, with HZ specimens slightly stronger and of similar elongation. Despite a bulk density above 99.9%, micro-CT revealed isolated pores of roughly 60–270 μm. At 600 MPa, VT specimens failed after 6.79 × 104 and 7.36 × 104 cycles, whereas HZ specimens failed after 8.82 × 105 and 1.37 × 106 cycles. Fatigue data at other stress levels are limited, so the orientation effect is demonstrated only at 600 MPa, where two specimens per orientation were tested. The results indicate that defect size, morphology, and orientation relative to the load, rather than tensile properties or density, are the likely cause of the anisotropy. An orientation-sensitive descriptor, F = dmax cos2θ, is proposed as a hypothesis; specimen-resolved defect data exist for only three VT specimens, so it remains to be validated. No as-built control was tested, and conclusions apply to the annealed condition.</jats:p>
title: Defect-Related Fatigue Anisotropy in Laser Powder Bed Fusion Ti–6Al–4V: Role of Sub-β-Transus Annealing and Build Orientation

items.abstract:
<jats:p>Problem definition: Diagnostic discrepancies, defined as mismatches between patients’ admitting and principal diagnoses, are common but heterogeneous claims-based markers. These discrepancies represent a misalignment in the diagnostic process, reflecting diagnostic updating, reprioritization, residual clinical complexity, documentation practices, or error without establishing clinical preventability and may signal latent operational burden in subsequent physician decision making. We examine whether this retrospective operational flag identifies inpatient stays with larger adjusted resource-use differentials and whether those differentials vary with physician experience. Methodology/results: Leveraging a patient-level data set of 5.7 million emergency department–origin inpatient stays from Florida hospitals, we examine the operational burden associated with diagnostic discrepancies, measured by total costs per hospitalization. Our results show that discrepancy-flagged inpatient stays have 6.62% higher adjusted total cost after rich patient risk adjustment and high-dimensional fixed effects. The adjusted differential is smaller at higher focal experience (treating similar diagnoses) and larger at higher related experience (treating diverse diagnoses). The pattern remains qualitatively similar across alternative discrepancy definitions, richer diagnosis and service-line controls, risk-adjusted benchmarking, physician matching, alternative experience measures, and alternative samples. Exploratory analyses further show that flagged inpatient stays exhibit higher costs across multiple resource-use domains with varying intensity, higher diagnostic and procedural intensity, and longer adjusted time to first procedure. Managerial implications: The discrepancy flag is most appropriately used for retrospective monitoring, benchmarking, and case-review triage, not as a direct measure of preventable error or as an automatic performance score. The physician experience patterns motivate prospective evaluation of assignment, consultation, training, and decision-support practices.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>Funding: This research was supported by a 2024 Research Grant from the Center for Management Innovations in Healthcare and a 2024 Eller College Small Research Grant, both at the University of Arizona.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>Supplemental Material: The online appendix is available at https://doi.org/10.1287/msom.2025.0603 .</jats:p>
title: Operational Implications of Diagnostic Discrepancies: The Weigh-in of Focal and Related Physician Experience

<jats:p>Background Colorectal cancer (CRC) remains one of the leading causes of death worldwide because of its late detection which results from being asymptomatic in the early stages and poor adherence to the invasive screening procedure such as colonoscopy. The existing biomarkers used in the blood for early detection of this disease include carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) and carbohydrate antigen 19-9 (CA19-9), but they have poor sensitivity. Non-coding RNAs have proven to be key epigenetic factors for CRC progression and metastasis, including circular RNA ITCH (circITCH) and long non-coding RNA HOTAIR (lncRNA-HOTAIR).
Methods In a case-control study on 200 subjects (120 CRC patients and 80 healthy controls) whose specimens were histopathologically confirmed, the expressions of circITCH and lncRNA-HOTAIR were analyzed using qRT-PCR along with CEA and CA19-9. There were conducted clinicopathological correlations, ROC curves and multiple logistic regression analysis.
Results Serum levels of circITCH were significantly lower in CRC patients than in healthy control group (0.54 ± 0.24 vs. 1.03 ± 0.31, P<0.001), whereas the level of lncRNA-HOTAIR was significantly higher (3.21 ± 1.38 vs. 1.06 ± 0.42, P<0.001). The individual AUCs of the biomarkers HOTAIR and circITCH were 0.941 (95% CI: 0.909–0.974) and 0.889 (95% CI: 0.840–0.938), respectively. The combined panel (circITCH + lncRNA-HOTAIR) showed superior diagnostic efficacy with the highest AUC of 0.969 (95% CI: 0.947–0.990; sensitivity= 93.3%; specificity= 91.3%), surpassing significantly the traditional protein biomarkers.
Conclusion Circulating levels of circITCH + lncRNA-HOTAIR display complementary expression profiles and, when combined serve as effective, minimally invasive diagnostic biomarkers for CRC.</jats:p>
title: Serum circITCH and lncRNA HOTAIR expression  signatures: Novel diagnostic and metastatic  biomarkers for colorectal cancer

items.abstract: <jats:p>Ectopic adrenal tissue in the liver is an uncommon condition. Based on this ectopic presence, adrenal hyperplasia, adenomas, or cancer may develop. If intrahepatic adrenal tissue is non-functional and does not cause clinical symptoms by compressing surrounding structures, it may be managed with follow-up observation without the need for further surgical treatment. In this case, however, because preoperative imaging was highly suggestive of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), surgical resection was ultimately performed to confirm the diagnosis and exclude malignancy. This article reports an uncommon case of intrahepatic adrenal cortical hyperplasia. We analyze the imaging and pathological characteristics of this lesion and discuss the corresponding diagnostic strategies.</jats:p>
title: Case Report: Intrahepatic ectopic adrenal cortical hyperplasia: a mimic of hepatocellular carcinoma and a diagnostic pitfall

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>This article presents an interview with Umberto Finzi, a plasma physicist and senior official of the European Commission who played a central role in the development of the European fusion programme from the late 1970s to the early 2000s. Through Finzi’s testimony, the article traces the evolution of nuclear fusion research in Europe from its early institutionalization within the EURATOM framework to the emergence of large-scale international projects such as the Joint European Torus (JET) and ITER. The interview offers a unique perspective at the intersection of science and policy, highlighting the institutional mechanisms, governance structures, and negotiation processes that shaped European fusion research. Particular attention is devoted to the EURATOM system of ‘Associations’, which enabled the coordination of a distributed network of national laboratories, and to the transition from a pluralistic research landscape to large-scale collaborative infrastructures. The article also examines the role of international negotiation and science diplomacy in the genesis of ITER, emphasizing how agreements were achieved through the expansion of the negotiation framework beyond strictly scientific and technical issues. Finzi’s account sheds light on the interplay between scientific objectives, engineering constraints, and political priorities, showing how large-scale projects emerge from complex processes of compromise and alignment among multiple actors. By situating this testimony within the historiography of fusion research and European integration, the article contributes to a deeper understanding of nuclear fusion as a field shaped not only by scientific and technological developments, but also by institutional innovation and international cooperation.</jats:p>
title: Negotiating fusion: European science policy and the making of ITER

items.abstract: <jats:p>With the development of Computed Tomography (CT), Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) and other medical imaging technologies, the image data is becoming more and more high-definition, three-dimensional, and the amount of data is increasing, which has brought pressure to hospital storage, transmission and remote diagnosis and treatment. Unlike ordinary image compression, medical image compression should not only pursue smaller files, but also ensure that the details related to diagnosis are not lost, that is, to ensure "diagnostic fidelity". This paper reviews the development process of medical image compression from traditional coding, region of interest compression, three-dimensional compression to deep learning compression, analyzes the characteristics and applicable scenarios of various methods, summarizes the cutting-edge directions of high-level deep data processing and cross scene adaptation combined with recent research, and finally points out the problems of current evaluation standards are not unified, the model is not universal enough, and gives the development ideas for clinical diagnosis.</jats:p>
title: From Traditional Transformation to Deep Learning: The Technical Evolution of Medical Image Compression and the Challenge of Diagnostic Fidelity
